papers.title: Leveraging genomic deep learning models for the prediction of noncoding variant effects.
papers.abstract: Characterizing noncoding variant function remains an important challenge in human genetics. Genomic deep learning models have emerged as a promising approach to enable in silico prediction of variant effects. These models include supervised sequence-to-activity models, which predict molecular phenotypes such as genome-wide chromatin states or gene expression levels directly from DNA sequence, and self-supervised genomic language models. Here we review progress in leveraging these models for noncoding variant effect prediction. We describe practical considerations for making such predictions and categorize the types of ground-truth data used to evaluate variant effect predictions, providing insight into the settings in which current models are most useful. Our Review highlights key considerations for practitioners and opportunities for improvement in model development and evaluation.

papers.title: Circuit-aligned specialization of human basal ganglia astrocytes.
papers.abstract: Astrocytes shape synapses and circuits, yet their diversity within the human basal ganglia remains poorly defined. Integrating single-nucleus transcriptomic and epigenomic profiling with spatial transcriptomics, we identify three anatomically organized astrocyte subgroups-striatal gray matter (GM), extra-striatal GM, and white matter (WM)-distinguished by neurotransmitter transporter expression and synapse-associated programs that reflect afferent input. These molecular distinctions generalize brain-wide, separating telencephalic from non-telencephalic astrocytes, with LHX2 marking telencephalic astrocyte identity across species. Within the striatum (STR), dorsal and ventral populations align with distinct microcircuits; a ventral population maps to the nucleus accumbens mediodorsal shell alongside specialized neuronal subtypes, a pattern conserved in nonhuman primates. A deep learning sequence model identifies subgroup-specific enhancer codes and recovers established transcription factor motif logic from published enhancer-AAV datasets, providing a foundation for targeted viral vector design. These findings define intersecting axes of human astrocyte specialization and offer a framework for cell-type-specific dissection of basal ganglia circuits.

papers.title: LitGene: an interpretable transformer model integrating text and ontology for gene representation learning.
papers.abstract: Representation learning in genomics often relies on sequence, expression, and network data, thereby overlooking a wealth of insights in the scientific literature. Here, we present LitGene, an interpretable transformer-based model that refines gene representations by integrating unstructured textual information with Gene Ontology annotations through contrastive learning. In evaluations across eight benchmark tasks for protein properties, LitGene achieves competitive accuracy and exhibits zero-shot prediction of GO terms, KEGG pathways, and gene-disease associations. LitGene identified ANGPTL6 as a potential candidate gene for idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), supported by its differential expression in independent IPF samples, illustrating LitGene's utility for hypothesis generation. A SHAP-based interpretability tool highlights text features influencing predictions, while an automated literature-grounding framework provides corroborating support where available. Our results suggest that integrating textual and genetic information may help reduce biases associated with under-studied genes. The model is released as open-source code, along with a publicly accessible web interface at https://litgene.cs.unm.edu/ , which allows users to submit gene names, disease names, drug names, or custom text (e.g., publication abstracts) to obtain evidence-based predictions of related biomedical entities.

papers.title: A Three-Axis Framework for Therapy Prioritization in MBD4-Deficient Tumors: De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Modeling, Replication-Stress Pharmacology, and PARP1 Trapping Decoupling
papers.abstract: Background: Loss-of-function mutations in MBD4 (methyl-CpG-binding domain protein 4) cause a specialized base excision repair (BER) deficiency characterized by hypermutated CpG>TpG signatures and sensitivity to immune checkpoint blockade. However, post-immunotherapy treatment prioritization remains empirically unmapped. In clinical oncology, DNA damage response (DDR) defects are frequently extrapolated to poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase inhibitor (PARPi) sensitivity by analogy to homologous recombination deficiency (HRD), without testing whether upstream glycosylase loss generates the nicked single-strand break (SSB) intermediates required for toxic PARP1-DNA trapping. Methods: We developed a three-axis framework integrating mechanistic curation, large-scale pharmacogenomics (DepMap 24Q2 CRISPR/RNA-seq, n=1,517; GDSC2 dose-response profiling, n=928; PRISM Repurposing), and a 5-Layer De-confounded Synthetic Lethality Machine Learning (SL-ML) Engine (SL-XGBRanker). To prevent functional dilution from variants of uncertain significance, MBD4 loss-of-function (MBD4-LOF) was strictly restricted to truncating and canonical splice-site alleles (21 of 36 mutated lines), independently validated by nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD; two-sided p2s = 0.0367), while excluding 15 lines harboring 19 non-truncating variants (18 missense, 1 inframe deletion). All primary pharmacogenomic comparisons were evaluated using two-sided Mann-Whitney U tests (p2s), bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs), Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (BH-FDR) multiplicity correction across six pre-specified candidate axes, and Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) for expression equivalence. Results: Our analysis delineates three distinct therapeutic axes in MBD4-LOF tumors: (1) Cytidine Analog Vulnerability (Axis 1): Mechanistic structural evidence demonstrates that MBD4 loss impairs excision of 5-substituted pyrimidine analogs and deaminated bases, creating a direct biochemical bottleneck to gemcitabine and 5-fluorouracil incorporation. (2) ATR-Check1 Replication-Stress Vulnerability (Axis 2): In GDSC2 profiling, MBD4-LOF cell lines exhibit significant sensitivity to the ATR inhibitor ceralasertib (AZD6738). In the clinically relevant TP53-mutant background-which disables the G1/S checkpoint and forces reliance on ATR-mediated S/G2 arrest-MBD4-LOF lines (n=11 vs n=619 WT) demonstrate pronounced ceralasertib hypersensitivity (Delta LN_IC50 = -1.07, 95% CI [-1.62, -0.41], Cohen's d = -0.74, p2s = 0.0060, BH-FDR q = 0.036; Delta AUC = -0.087, d = -0.89, p2s = 0.0017), with 11/11 leave-one-out (LOO) jackknife iterations retaining two-sided significance (p2s <= 0.014). This genotype-associated dependency remains robust in the unstratified pan-cancer cohort (n=14 vs n=914 WT; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.73, 95% CI [-1.31, -0.11], d = -0.50, p2s = 0.0430; Delta AUC = -0.056, d = -0.56, p2s = 0.0259) and after purging microsatellite instability-high (MSI-H) lines (n=10 vs n=906 WT MSS; Delta LN_IC50 = -0.9

papers.title: HyperGenie: A method for predicting enzymatic gene essentiality using hypergraph neural networks and genome-scale metabolic models
papers.abstract: Identifying essential genes in bacteria is crucial for drug discovery and synthetic biology. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) evaluated via flux balance analysis remain standard, yet they rely on the often-invalid premise that mutant strains optimize for maximum growth. Recent machine learning approaches circumvent this limitation using random forests or graph neural networks on mass flow graphs (MFGs). However, data-driven tools like random forests discard network topology, while graph-based tools like MFGs decompose multi-component biochemical reactions into pairwise interactions, misrepresenting complex stoichiometry and limiting interpretability. Furthermore, existing methods remain largely uncharacterised in data-scarce regimes and cross-environmental conditions. Here, we introduce HyperGenie, a framework that integrates genome-scale metabolic models with directed hypergraph neural networks by representing metabolites as nodes and reactions as hyperedges. Operating directly on wild-type flux features, HyperGenie eliminates post-knockout optimality assumptions, achieves a 13% PR-AUC improvement over prior objective-dependent methods, and matches computationally demanding, state-of-the-art flux-sampling baselines. Using HyperGenie to guide targeted growth curve assays, we identified latent essentiality misannotations across three genes in the benchmark iML1515 dataset, which we then reconciled and validated experimentally via PCR. In data-scarce regimes, HyperGenie retained robust predictive performance (> 90% PR-AUC) when trained on as little as 40% of the data. To isolate the value of hypergraph message passing, we benchmarked HyperGenie against an independent-reaction multilayer perceptron (MLPGenie) across diverse nutrient environments and uptake rates, where HyperGenie's hypergraph inductive bias yielded consistent accuracy gains (> 2% in glucose; > 4% across six alternative carbon sources). Notably, HyperGenie exhibits robust zero-shot cross-nutrient generalization, accurately forecasting gain-of-essentiality phenotypes on novel carbon sources, though loss-of-essentiality remains challenging. Finally, coupling hypergraph representations with SHAP attribution provides actionable mechanistic insights into metabolic rewiring, establishing a data-efficient, interpretable platform for discovering novel antibiotic targets.

papers.title: ProFormer: generalizable classification of single-cell and plasma proteomes using deep learning.
papers.abstract: Proteins are the main drivers of cell function and disease, making proteomics a powerful technique for biomarker discovery and defining cell identity. While current technologies can profile thousands of proteins and reach single-cell sensitivity, limited throughput restricts applications such as robust classification of large biological or clinical cohorts. To close this gap, we present a deep-learning (DL) approach for the direct analysis of mass spectrometric (MS) data, assigning proteomic profiles to sample identity. Specifically, we introduce the ProFormer, a transformer pipeline that classifies samples by tabular MS1-level features derived from peptide ions, eliminating the need for time-consuming data interpretation. The ProFormer outperforms traditional machine-learning and image-based convolutional neural networks (CNNs), demonstrating enhanced classification and generalization over 14 evaluated architectures. We further provide detailed insights into how the ProFormer dynamically aggregates MS1 data, while preserving signal contribution and enabling explainable AI at single-peptide resolution. Applied to diverse LC-MS data sets, the ProFormer accurately classified single-cell proteomes by cell type, cycle stage or differentiation trajectory, as well as patient disease status from plasma proteomes. Thereby, the ProFormer provides a versatile and rapid framework for the classification of proteomic data, with important implications for patient stratification, early detection and single-cell analysis.

papers.title: Multi-Assay Antibody Developability Prediction with Shared Structure-Language Representations
papers.abstract: Early assessment of antibody developability is critical in drug discovery, but computational approaches remain limited by the scarcity of experimental data. We explore two strategies for working within that limit. First, we designed per-residue physicochemical descriptors encoding the local structural environment, including new terms such as directional charge asymmetry and screened electrostatic potential. These feed a convolutional network, combined with protein language model (PLM) embeddings in a two-stream architecture: the two are encoded and predicted independently and merged only at the prediction stage. Second, a shared trunk with per-assay heads passes information between related assays. Both are implemented in the Multi-Assay Developability Model (MADM) and evaluated on eight assays: HIC, heparin affinity (HAC), AC-SINS, and polyspecificity ELISA against BVP, dsDNA, insulin, ovalbumin and soluble membrane proteins (SMP), with labels from 29 open sources. Structural descriptors match or exceed PLM embeddings (AbLang2, ESM2) on several assays; combining the streams gives a small but consistent gain in accuracy and reduces seed-to-seed variance. Multi-assay training raises Spearman rho for ovalbumin and SMP by about 0.1, where assays correlate and share sequence space. Under cluster-split cross-validation the strongest results are for HAC, ovalbumin, insulin, SMP and HIC (rho = 0.70-0.82); AC-SINS, BVP and dsDNA are weaker (0.50-0.55). In these three, sequence clusters largely coincide with data source, so a held-out fold measures transfer to differently calibrated measurements as well as to new sequences. On the 80-antibody GDPa3 hold-out, performance falls by rho around 0.1 for all but SMP (0.22). Transfer to the VHH panel of Ginkgo GDPa5 gives comparable results, and scFv validation against binary SMP labels yields F1 = 0.89, AUC = 0.95.

papers.title: OpenDVP: an experimental and computational framework for community-empowered deep visual proteomics.
papers.abstract: Deep visual proteomics (DVP) is an emerging approach for cell-type-specific and spatially resolved proteomics. However, its broad adoption has been constrained by the lack of an open-source end-to-end workflow within a community-driven ecosystem. Here we introduce openDVP, an experimental and computational framework for accessible and scalable DVP. OpenDVP combines open-source image analysis tools (MCMICRO, QuPath and napari) with scverse formats (AnnData and SpatialData) for multiomics integration. It provides two workflows: a fast-track pipeline requiring no image analysis expertise, and an artificial intelligence-powered pipeline incorporating state-of-the-art methods for image preprocessing, segmentation and spatial analysis. We apply openDVP across three archival tissue studies (human placenta, early stage lung cancer and locally relapsed breast cancer), integrating spatial single-cell phenotypes with exploratory proteomic measurements. Finally, we introduce deep proteomic profiling of cellular neighborhoods as a scalable approach for spatial discovery proteomics.

papers.title: An integrative single-cell epigenomic atlas annotates the regulatory genome of the adult mouse brain.
papers.abstract: Histone modifications underpin the cell-type-specific gene regulatory programs that drive the remarkable cellular diversity of the mammalian brain. Here, we jointly profiled four histone modifications and the transcriptome in 2.5 million nuclei from the adult mouse brain. By integrating these data with chromatin accessibility, DNA methylation, and three-dimensional genome organization, we constructed a unified epigenomic atlas spanning over 100 brain cell subclasses and assigned active, primed, and repressive chromatin states across 81% of the genome. Active chromatin states marked by combinatorial histone modifications better nominate candidate enhancers with functional support than chromatin accessibility alone, while H3K27me3- and H3K9me3-marked chromatin states delineate distinct modes of cell-type-specific gene repression. Finally, this multimodal resource enables the development of deep learning models that predict cell-type-specific epigenomic features and gene expression from DNA sequence, providing a comprehensive framework for annotating the brain regulatory genome and interpreting non-coding disease risk variants.

papers.title: Weight locking as a safeguard for open-weight biological foundation models
papers.abstract: Biological foundation models can accelerate research, but their open weight release raises biosecurity concerns. A common safeguard excludes eukaryotic viral genomes from training, but fine-tuning on public viral data reverses it. We confirm that fine-tuning improves held-out viral language modelling, and that the gain comes from the viral data itself. Weight locking by spectral deformation, proposed to prevent fine-tuning, is untested in biological models. We applied it to two Evo-family models and the protein model ESM3-open, against attackers of increasing knowledge. The lock defends against the naive attacker, whose fine-tuning drives capability below pretrained on all three models. It does not defend against an informed attacker, who freezes or fuses the compensation matrix to restore near-unlocked performance. A compensation-free lock we build from the network's own rescaling symmetries again defeats the naive attacker, but canonical rebalancing removes it without knowledge of the lock. The barrier is one of knowledge, not compute.

papers.title: Deep learning-based enhancing spatial biological context parsing.
papers.abstract: The rapid advancement of spatial transcriptomics (ST) has established a foundation for the complementary integration of multimodal information from gene expression profiles, spatial localization, and histological images. However, noise and data heterogeneity complicate the characterization of spatial relationships and tissue structure. In this study, we develop a deep learning framework, CroSP, based on a multi-view graph autoencoder. The framework integrates gene expression profiles, spatial locations, and tissue morphology information into a low-dimensional latent representation. Cross-view contrastive learning and metric learning coordinate the complementary views. Across datasets from multiple platforms and spatial resolutions, CroSP improved spatial domain identification and delineated brain and olfactory bulb structures. Analyses using established downstream methods further characterized spatially variable genes and the spatial heterogeneity, immune microenvironments, and cell-cell communication in human breast cancer tissue. These results support the use of CroSP for spatial biological analysis in healthy and diseased tissues. Source code and tutorials: https://github.com/Biowust/CroSP.git. Archived code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22675113. Public raw datasets: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22533825.

papers.title: Impact of data quality on deep learning prediction of spatial transcriptomics from histology images.
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomic technologies enable high-throughput quantification of gene expression at specific locations across tissue sections, facilitating insights into the spatial organization of biological processes. However, high costs associated with these technologies have motivated the development of deep learning methods to predict spatial gene expression from inexpensive hematoxylin and eosin-stained histology images. While most efforts have focused on modifying model architectures to boost predictive performance, the influence of training data quality remains largely unexplored. Here, we investigate how variation in molecular and image data quality stemming from differences in spatial transcriptomic technologies impact deep learning-based gene expression prediction from histology images. To identify the aspects of data quality that impact predictive performance, we conduct in silico ablation experiments, which show that increased sparsity and noise in molecular data degrade predictive performance, while in silico rescue experiments via imputation provide only limited improvements that fail to generalize beyond the test set. Likewise, reduced image resolution can degrade predictive performance and further impacts model interpretability. We further demonstrate that these data quality-driven effects are reproducible across multiple spatial transcriptomics technologies and tissues, and remain consistent when using alternative feature extractors and model architectures. Overall, our results show how improving data quality provides an orthogonal strategy to tuning model architecture in spatial transcriptomics-based predictive modeling, highlighting the need to account for technology-specific limitations that directly impact data quality when developing predictive methodologies.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Protein-Ligand Binding Site Prediction from Protein Sequence and SMILES
papers.abstract: Accurate identification of protein-ligand binding sites is critical for mechanistic biology and drug discovery, yet predictive performance varies substantially across ligand families and data-availability regimes. We present a systematic ligand-aware benchmark and evaluation framework for residue-level binding-site prediction across three settings: overrepresented ligands with abundant examples, underrepresented ligands with limited examples, and zero-shot ligands unseen during training. Using a BioLiP2-derived dataset with ligand-specific sequence clustering, we evaluate a progressive three-stage sequence-based modeling suite designed to study these regimes. Stage 1 trains ligand-specific predictors using a pretrained protein language model (PLM). Stage 2 introduces ligand conditioning through learned embeddings, enabling a single multi-ligand model. Stage 3 replaces these embeddings with representations from a pretrained chemical language model (CLM) operating on SMILES, enabling prediction for previously unseen ligands. In the original three-stage comparison, Stage 2 achieved a higher ligand-macro F1 than Stage 1 on the overrepresented test set (0.5832 versus 0.4769), although the comparison simultaneously changes predictor architecture, ligand conditioning, and the training regime. Stage 2 also outperformed several sequence- and structure-based baselines. Stage 3 achieves a pooled residue-level F1 of 0.3109 and a ligand-macro F1 of 0.2338 on previously unseen ligands, while remaining competitive on represented ligands. Control experiments using constant, mismatched, and scrambled SMILES inputs reduce performance across all three test regimes, providing evidence that the model uses information associated with the supplied ligand input rather than relying solely on generic protein binding-site propensity. Ablations across five PLM scales and multiple CLMs further show that increasing PLM scale generally improves performance, although the trend is not strictly monotonic, whereas CLM scaling produces smaller and less consistent gains. Overall, this study provides a systematic benchmark for quantifying the effect of ligand data availability on residue-level binding-site prediction and for evaluating generalization to previously unseen ligands.

papers.title: Benchmarking generative AI tools for literature retrieval and summarization in genomic variant interpretation.
papers.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to extract structured information across domains, but its reliability in academic and clinical research, where precision and accuracy are essential, remains largely unexplored. This study evaluates the ability of Large Language Models based algorithms to generate accurate, literature-based summaries of human genomic variants, with a focus on real-world usability. We benchmark five open-access generative AI platforms-ChatGPT, MistralAI, VarChat, Perplexity, and ScholarAI-across 40 curated variants equally divided between somatic and germline settings. For each variant, summary reports are generated and blindly evaluated by domain experts using five defined metrics. VarChat emerges as the top-ranked tool, showing the highest summarization accuracy, citation relevance, and robustness against hallucinations. Gpt-4o consistently ranked second, showing particularly stable robustness in conditions where the literature was scarce. Perplexity and ScholarAI, despite being literature-focused, rank lowest across most metrics. Tool performance is strongly influenced by the availability of peer-reviewed literature, confirming that current generative models remain sensitive to data scarcity. Our findings highlight the heterogeneity of current generative AI tools in genomic variant interpretation workflows. While some platforms already provide useful outputs, reliable integration into basic and clinical research requires expert validation and domain-related fine-tuning. This work provides a first systematic expert-evaluation framework for benchmarking large language model-generated content in variant genomics and underscores the need for caution when using these tools to support variant interpretation.

papers.title: Mapping Gene-by-Environment Interactions via the Plasma Exposome at Cell-Type Resolution
papers.abstract: Gene-by-environment (GxE) interactions inform where genetics and environment converge to impact human health and disease. However, systematically mapping GxE interactions has been challenging due to the diversity of testable exposures and a lack of scalable approaches to measure the environments cells experience in vivo. Here, we identified modules of correlated plasma metabolites and proteins and used them as quantitative proxies for environmental exposures experienced by circulating leukocytes. We demonstrated that these proxies are associated with environmentally modifiable clinical traits such as diet and infection and support broad mapping of geneby environment (GxE) interactions affecting gene expression and CpG methylation in leukocytes. We identified significant interactions for 95.2% of tested genes and 5.9% of tested methylation sites. These GxE interactions showed specificity to exposures and cell type. Colocalization analysis further provided links between interactions and complex trait and disease loci. Finally, we expanded GxE interaction mapping to unexplored cell types using a zero-shot transfer model to predict GxE interactions in held-out cell types, demonstrating how plasma metabolomics and proteomics can enhance the discovery of GxE interactions across the body. Altogether, this work provides a systematic multi-omic framework to study how gene regulation is shaped by both the genome and the molecular environments cells experience in vivo.

papers.title: Omics-scale decoding of protein N-glycosylation using protein language model embeddings
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) learn rich sequence semantics from vast volume of protein sequences, yet the information encoded in their high-dimensional embeddings remains largely a black box, posing an interpretability challenge. Here we show that semantic features learned by pLMs can be decoded to reveal biologically meaningful signals using coevolutionary analysis without downstream supervised-training. Building on this insight, we developed MaskNGly, a zero-shot framework that identifies protein N-glycosylation sites directly from PLM-embeddings while achieving performance comparable to state-of-the-art supervised predictors. MaskNGly is computationally efficient and intrinsically transferable, enabling omics-scale characterization of protein glycosylation landscape. Applied across proteomes, it reveals that canonical N-X-S/T motifs gain higher glycosylation propensities with increasing organismal complexity and that glycosylation preferentially occurs at structured, solvent-exposed regions. Mutations altering high-scoring motifs are more frequently disease-associated. The framework also captures signatures of glycosylation-mediated protein allostery. These results establish an interpretable and scalable route to study glycobiology from pLM-embeddings.

papers.title: DRAFT: graph-recurrent learning of dynamic gene regulatory networks along single-cell multi-omics trajectories
papers.abstract: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation. Here we present DRAFT, a deep learning framework that combines graph attention with recurrent temporal memory to infer dynamic GRNs from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics data. On simulated data, DRAFT outperforms existing methods in accuracy and temporal smoothness. In mouse cellular reprogramming and Drosophila adult spermatogenesis, it recovers interactions supported by independent ChIP-seq, perturbation and Hi-C data, together with known stage-specific regulators. By inferring regulatory activity from dynamic network structure rather than expression alone, DRAFT identifies regulators whose activity precedes their transcriptional peak, including the candidate early germline regulator Mondo. Germline-specific Mondo knockdown alters germline stem cell number and expression of the predicted targets kuz and mamo. DRAFT also enables nonlinear alignment of co-developing lineages and reveals stage-specific cell-cell communication.

papers.title: DecoyOpt: A two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction
papers.abstract: Accurate and efficient EC number prediction is essential for elucidating the catalytic roles of enzymes. Although similarity-based and deep learning-based approaches have advanced this task, they often fail to distinguish active enzymes from closely related decoys inactivated by local functional-site mutations, leading to high false-positive rates (FPRs). We propose DecoyOpt, a two-stage pipeline for decoy-aware enzyme discrimination and EC number prediction. Specifically, we generated putatively inactive functional-site decoys using ESM3 and evaluated 16 protein language models across three splits. An MLP trained with classification and ranking losses distinguishes enzymes from unannotated proteins and decoys before a contrastive learning model assigns EC numbers to predicted enzymes. On the most stringent GraphPart 40% split, DecoyOpt achieves an MCC of 0.899 and a D0 decoy FPR of 6.17%, outperforming retrained baselines. Across all splits, it outperforms these baselines in EC number prediction on the full test set while maintaining performance close to CLEAN on the enzyme subset. It also correctly annotates all four wild-type enzymes and rejects all eight inactive or nearly inactive variants. We believe that DecoyOpt has potential for annotating uncharacterized proteins and their variants, with applications in genomics, synthetic biology, and biocatalysis.

papers.title: HINN prioritizes multi-omics biomarkers associated with cognitive decline.
papers.abstract: Integrating multi-omics data for disease prediction remains challenging due to the complexity of cross-layer biological interactions and the limited use of prior biological knowledge in many machine learning models. We present the Hierarchical Input Neural Network (HINN), a deep learning framework that incorporates biologically informed connections across genomic, epigenetic, and transcriptomic layers to model regulatory relationships in a structured and interpretable manner. HINN was applied to blood-derived multi-omics data to predict cognitive assessment scores, including Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Montreal Cognitive Assessment, Alzheimer's Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale 11 tasks (ADAS11), and Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test. A biologically guided feature construction pipeline was used to integrate genome-wide association studies-derived single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), promoter-region DNA methylation, and gene expression data through Gene Ontology Biological Process and KEGG pathway mappings. The model was evaluated using a rigorous training strategy that separates feature selection from testing and incorporates cross-validation as well as repeated runs to ensure robustness. Across all cognitive outcomes, HINN achieved the lowest mean normalized mean squared error among the evaluated models, with statistically significant improvements over most baseline methods. Ablation analyses showed that the contributions of individual omics modalities and biologically informed connectivity varied across cognitive outcomes, with the clearest benefits of structured connectivity observed for ADAS11 and MMSE. Feature attribution analysis identified a multi-omics cascade involving SNP (rs116557230), CpG site (cg24041822), and a SOCS4 gene expression probe, which showed consistent associations with multiple cognitive outcomes. These findings highlight the ability of HINN to uncover biologically meaningful cross-omics relationships relevant to cognitive decline. Together, this work demonstrates that integrating deep learning with biological knowledge enables biomarker discovery for complex diseases. All code, sample data, and instructions are publicly available via GitHub (https://github.com/bozdaglab/HINN) and archived on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19197057) to ensure reproducibility and long-term accessibility.

papers.title: Decoding Cell-type Specific Gene Regulation with CellReg3D by Integrating DNA Large Language Models and 3D Genome Structure
papers.abstract: Gene regulation is a core biological mechanism crucial for organismal growth and development. Recent advances in deep learning, coupled with increasing computational resources, have enabled large-scale modelling of gene regulatory processes. While numerous models have been proposed, effectively capturing long-range genomic interactions remains a central challenge. Here, we introduce CellReg3D, a multiscale and multi-modal deep learning framework designed to model cell-type-specific gene regulation by integrating local sequence patterns with long-range genomic interactions. Existing approaches often overlook the contribution of 3D genome architecture and face limitations in combining sequence-based features with chromatin interaction data. Specifically, CellReg3D overcomes these gaps by leveraging a DNA language model to encode sequence-level information and incorporating Hi-C-derived 3D chromatin interactions to capture chromatin spatial organization. We demonstrate that CellReg3D effectively learns epigenetic patterns and chromatin activity states, achieving state-of-the-art performance in predicting epigenetic marks and gene expression profiles across multiple cell types. Using interpretable methods, we illustrate how the model identifies cell-type-specific regulatory mechanisms and prioritizes functional non-coding variants. Furthermore, we apply CellReg3D to enhance the interpretation of expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and uncover novel potential gene regulatory interactions. Overall, CellReg3D offers a integrative framework for decoding regulatory genomics, unifying sequence and 3D genome structure data to advance variant prioritization, disease mechanism discovery, and personalized functional genomics.

papers.title: Generation of protein conformations using a simple inverted transformer
papers.abstract: Molecular dynamics is an extremely powerful approach for studying protein behavior, but it requires enormous computational resources to obtain an adequate sampling of possible conformations. Recently, thanks to successes in predicting three-dimensional protein structures, there has been an explosion of research exploring the opportunities offered by deep learning to address the problem of protein conformational landscape. In this work, an artificial intelligence system based on a variant of the Transformer architecture is introduced and applied to the problem of determining the ensemble of three-dimensional structures that a protein can access and their statistical weight. After being trained on a dataset of conformations of a particular protein obtained using classical all-atom molecular dynamics, this neural network is able to directly generate physically plausible protein conformations similar to those obtained both through molecular dynamics and experimentally. The ordered sequence of conformations obtained as output of the neural network rapidly converges towards the most populated regions of the protein's conformational landscape, suggesting that the system may have learned not only the protein's three-dimensional organization but also the thermodynamic weights of the various feasible conformations. These features, combined with its simplicity and low computational load, make this Transformer variant an ideal candidate for the development of systems capable of performing generative molecular dynamics.

papers.title: Decompose and Recompose: Reference-Centered Multimodal Adaptation of Protein Language Models for Enzyme Turnover Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting enzyme turnover numbers ($k_{\mathrm{cat}}$) from protein sequences and reaction chemistry helps prioritize candidates in virtual screening. Reliable ranking requires distinguishing activity differences between enzyme--reaction pairs. Recent interaction models combine enzyme and chemical information, but two representation challenges remain. First, reactants and products have distinct roles in catalysis: reactants are recognized and transformed, whereas products are formed and released. Yet these models merge the two sides before enzyme interaction, leaving the enzyme's response to each role implicit. Second, enzyme representations produced by cross-attention mix reaction-dependent changes with an enzyme-specific background shared across chemical conditions. This mixture can obscure activity-relevant differences between samples. To address these challenges, we introduce EnzRef, a lightweight multimodal framework that adapts frozen protein language models by decomposing reaction chemistry into reactant and product conditions, expressing each conditioned enzyme response relative to that enzyme's background, and recomposing the responses for activity prediction. Reference-Centered Cross-Attention uses each enzyme's average residue response as an internal reference to expose role-specific conditional deviations. Symmetry-Aware Semantic Recomposition encodes the mean deviation and directed role contrast into a joint activity representation. With 1.72M trainable parameters beyond the frozen encoder, EnzRef achieves state-of-the-art source-domain prediction on CatPred-DB and zero-shot transfer to TurNuP-DB. On unseen enzymes, it improves mean $R^2$ by 19.8% relative to MCKcat, the strongest baseline, without target-domain adaptation.

papers.title: A Proteome-Wide Gain-of-Function Atlas Mapping the Landscape of Chemotherapy Response
papers.abstract: Background: Conventional chemotherapies remain the core therapeutic backbone of cancer treatment, yet the rapid emergence of chemoresistance often compromises their clinical efficacy. Although large-scale functional genomics has transformed precision oncology, existing reference maps rely predominantly on loss-of-function paradigms and lack systematic data on gain-of-function (GOF) events that commonly drive clinical resistance. Methods: To address this gap, we engineered a site-specific Bxb1 integrase landing-pad system in HeLa cells, enabling single-copy integration of a human proteome-wide library [18,388 open reading frames (ORFs)] at the AAVS1 locus under a uniform EF1 promoter. We systematically profiled cellular fitness across 16 chemotherapeutics. We integrated this GOF perturbation screen with bulk and single-cell RNA sequencing, FACS-based lysosomal functional screening, clinical cohort survival analyses, and preclinical xenograft modeling. Results: Stratified modeling of over 230,000 gene-drug interactions defined distinct functional categories that are strongly enriched for clinical cancer biomarkers and prognostic relevance. Global network analysis and organelle-specific lysosomal functional screening uncovered that chemotherapeutic agents, most prominently the nucleoside analog TAS-102 (Lonsurf), converge upon a shared survival hub centered on the BCL-2 family-associated autophagy-endolysosomal network. Mechanistically, TAS-102 triggered lysosomal activation as an adaptive survival response. Co-treatment with the BCL-2 family inhibitor ABT-263 (Navitoclax) attenuated this TAS-102-induced lysosomal response and synergistically reversed TAS-102 resistance across colorectal and pancreatic cancer models in vitro and in colorectal cell line- and patient-derived xenograft (CDX, PDX) models in vivo. Conclusions: Our study establishes an open-access, proteome-wide GOF reference atlas that systematically maps chemotherapeutic responses, recapitulates canonical resistance biology, and nominates rational drug combinations. This systems-genomics resource bridges massive-scale perturbation mapping with actionable target discovery, providing a translational framework to overcome therapeutic resistance and reprogram cancer drug responses.

papers.title: Artificial intelligence in multi-omics data integration: Advancing precision medicine, biomarker discovery and genomic-driven disease interventions
papers.abstract: The integration of multi-omics data—encompassing genomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, and metabolomics—has revolutionized biomedical research, offering unprecedented insights into disease mechanisms and therapeutic interventions. However, the complexity and volume of multi-omics datasets present significant analytical challenges that traditional computational methods struggle to address. Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning and neural networks, has emerged as a powerful tool to overcome these limitations by enabling advanced data integration, biomarker discovery, and personalized treatment strategies. This paper explores the role of AI-driven multi-omics data integration in enhancing disease prediction, early diagnosis, and precision medicine. By leveraging AI models such as deep neural networks (DNNs), convolutional neural networks (CNNs), and transformers, researchers can analyze complex biological interactions, identify patterns indicative of disease onset, and stratify patient populations for tailored treatment approaches. Additionally, AI-powered feature selection methods facilitate the identification of disease-specific biomarkers across multiple omics layers, paving the way for more effective targeted therapies. Moreover, AI plays a crucial role in pharmacogenomics by predicting individualized drug responses, optimizing dosage regimens, and minimizing adverse drug reactions. Machine learning algorithms, including reinforcement learning and generative models, enable real-time modeling of drug-gene interactions, leading to safer and more efficacious therapeutic interventions. Despite the transformative potential of AI in multi-omics data analysis, challenges such as data standardization, model interpretability, and ethical considerations must be addressed to ensure reliability and clinical applicability. This paper provides a comprehensive review of AI-driven multi-omics research, highlighting current advancements, challenges, and future directions in precision medicine.
papers.venue: International Journal of Science and Research Archive

papers.title: Re-timing mortality risk through individualized modelling of lifespan trajectories.
papers.abstract: There is an urgent global need for affordable, large-scale health screening to enhance preventive care in the ageing population. Using low-cost, non-invasive retinal photographs and leveraging large foundation models, we developed a deep learning-based biomarker, Retinal Mortality Equivalent (RetiME), that directly mapped retinal features to individual mortality risk. Trained on a European cohort and externally validated across three independent external cohorts spanning Southeast Asia, Eurasia and North America, RetiME showed robust associations with all-cause and cause-specific mortality and predicted the incidence of a wide range of systemic and ocular diseases. Crucially, beyond static risk estimation, RetiME re-timed mortality risk by reconstructing personalized lifespan trajectories that were associated with observed mortality outcomes (for example, age of death). Clustering of these trajectories revealed distinct mortality patterns, spanning cancer-predominant, cardiometabolic and neurodegenerative risks, reflecting diverse ageing pathways captured by RetiME. Interpretability analyses showed that RetiME captures diverse biological and retinal features underlying mortality risk. Genome-wide analyses further identified genetic loci associated with RetiME. Collectively, these findings support further evaluation of retinal imaging and trajectory modelling as one component of a comprehensive assessment of mortality risk.

papers.title: More Genes, Faster Inference: Efficient Large-Panel Spatial Transcriptomics Prediction from Histology
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) prediction from histology aims to infer spatially resolved gene expression profiles directly from tissue images. This is a challenging problem that is currently often addressed with complicated model architectures, additional inputs, and complicated training procedures, while remaining limited to fixed, small gene panels. This raises a natural question: Is there an efficient method for large-panel ST prediction? Here, we present GeneFlow, a simpler yet effective framework for large-scale spatial gene expression prediction that unifies flow-matching generative modeling with structured multimodal fusion. Specifically, GeneFlow first encodes both histological morphology and cross-gene interactions in spatial spots through histology and gene tokenizers. The model directly predicts spatial gene expression, rather than an intermediate velocity field, while being trained with a velocity-based flow-matching objective. We show that, even without relying on heavy generative pipelines, GeneFlow achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple ST benchmarks, with up to 56.8% gains in 1,000-gene prediction. Extensive experiments further show that GeneFlow produces biologically meaningful spot profiles while reducing computational cost by orders of magnitude, thereby improving efficiency and scalability, particularly in clinical settings. We believe GeneFlow provides an opportunity for leveraging widely available histology images for downstream biological discovery. Code is available at: https://github.com/ZZhangsm/GeneFlow

papers.title: ProtCOVER: Family-Aware Conformal Prediction for Variant Effect Predictors on Unseen Protein Families
papers.abstract: Protein language models and related variant effect predictors (VEPs) increasingly classify missense variants in proteins evolutionarily distant from those used for calibration. Split conformal prediction over variants is valid for its own target, a random variant dominated by well-studied families, but deployment needs coverage for a variant of a new family. On ProteinGym clinical substitutions with five zero-shot predictors, Mondrian conformal comes within 0.005 of that target for four predictors, yet family-weighted pathogenic coverage is only 0.823-0.873 at a 0.90 target for all five, without any shift. We present ProtCOVER, a conformal procedure that treats homology families, rather than individual variants, as the exchangeable unit. ProtCOVER (i) calibrates at the family level over label-free homology clusters, giving marginal coverage for a new family under family exchangeability; (ii) adapts to descriptor shift by calibrating conditionally on an estimated density ratio of label-free descriptors (sequence similarity, alignment depth and embedding distance; a variant reweights by the ratio instead), with finite-sample family-weighted coverage, valid as computed, whenever the true ratio is a nonnegative affine function of the estimate; and (iii) can abstain at low effective calibration support, which proved no better than random abstention. Under a shift of its descriptors, ProtCOVER's mean worse-class shortfall below the target is 0.000, against 0.010 for group-weighted and 0.029 for hierarchical conformal prediction, with larger sets (about equal at matched coverage); on orphan families and held-out embedding regions it matches group weighting (0.002 against 0.003). In evaluations following pre-registered protocols, every shift-aware method met the target on new ClinVar variants of benchmark proteins, which ESM-1b separated better; on 12,225 proteins outside the benchmark, every method fell short for pathogenic variants with either of two predictors, ProtCOVER and a variant conditioned on the descriptors the least, within the 0.01 margin of group weighting.

papers.title: Opportunities for Artificial Intelligence in Advancing Precision Medicine
papers.abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: We critically evaluate the future potential of machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and artificial intelligence (AI) in precision medicine. The goal of this work is to show progress in ML in digital health, to exemplify future needs and trends, and to identify any essential prerequisites of AI and ML for precision health. RECENT FINDINGS: High-throughput technologies are delivering growing volumes of biomedical data, such as large-scale genome-wide sequencing assays; libraries of medical images; or drug perturbation screens of healthy, developing, and diseased tissue. Multi-omics data in biomedicine is deep and complex, offering an opportunity for data-driven insights and automated disease classification. Learning from these data will open our understanding and definition of healthy baselines and disease signatures. State-of-the-art applications of deep neural networks include digital image recognition, single-cell clustering, and virtual drug screens, demonstrating breadths and power of ML in biomedicine. SUMMARY: Significantly, AI and systems biology have embraced big data challenges and may enable novel biotechnology-derived therapies to facilitate the implementation of precision medicine approaches.

papers.title: Attribution-based diagnostics for single-cell foundation models
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA foundation models (scFMs) are increasingly used for in-silico biological discovery, yet predictive performance alone does not reveal whether their decisions rely on biologically meaningful signals or model-specific shortcuts. We systematically investigate post-hoc attribution of downstream predictions across two tasks: cell-type annotation using pretrained Cell2Sentence and scGPT models, and perturbation prediction using scGPT+STATE in a controlled setting. For cell annotation, we use attribution to assess whether predictions rely on established marker genes and how their relevance varies with model architecture, expression rank, and the surrounding cellular context. For perturbation prediction, we compare attribution patterns with known regulatory ground-truth in a synthetic setting to assess what they reveal about the model's learned computations. Across these tasks, attribution reveals biological feature use, contextual interactions, contributions from different input pathways, learning progression, associations with prediction quality, and potential pitfalls that are not fully captured by standard performance metrics. Experiments with complete and limited regulatory knowledge further demonstrate that conclusions drawn from attribution depend strongly on the choice of biological reference, baseline, and null model. Together, these findings highlight the value of attribution as a flexible post-hoc diagnostic for understanding model behavior, identifying potential issues, and informing the development of scFMs.

papers.title: ProteinBERT: a universal deep-learning model of protein sequence and function
papers.abstract: SUMMARY: Self-supervised deep language modeling has shown unprecedented success across natural language tasks, and has recently been repurposed to biological sequences. However, existing models and pretraining methods are designed and optimized for text analysis. We introduce ProteinBERT, a deep language model specifically designed for proteins. Our pretraining scheme combines language modeling with a novel task of Gene Ontology (GO) annotation prediction. We introduce novel architectural elements that make the model highly efficient and flexible to long sequences. The architecture of ProteinBERT consists of both local and global representations, allowing end-to-end processing of these types of inputs and outputs. ProteinBERT obtains near state-of-the-art performance, and sometimes exceeds it, on multiple benchmarks covering diverse protein properties (including protein structure, post-translational modifications and biophysical attributes), despite using a far smaller and faster model than competing deep-learning methods. Overall, ProteinBERT provides an efficient framework for rapidly training protein predictors, even with limited labeled data. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Code and pretrained model weights are available at https://github.com/nadavbra/protein_bert. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: SIREN: Predicting RNA-Small Molecule Interaction using Language Models without Requiring Structure
papers.abstract: RNA-targeted drug discovery is constrained by the scarcity of resolved RNA tertiary structures and the conformational flexibility of RNA, which limit the applicability of structure-based virtual screening. Here, SIREN (Small molecule Interaction with RNA via sEquence-based predictioN) is presented, a sequence-based framework that ranks small molecules for a given RNA target directly from its primary sequence without requiring tertiary structure. SIREN integrates a pretrained RNA language model with molecular language model embeddings and physicochemical descriptors through an interaction network that outputs a target-specific compound-ranking score. On four held-out ROBIN riboswitch targets, SIREN outperforms the structure-based methods RNAmigos2, RNAmigos++, and rDock in both enrichment and overall discrimination, and a cross-target derangement analysis confirms that its rankings depend on RNA identity rather than general ligand propensity alone. On an independent HIV-1 TAR benchmark, SIREN achieves strong discrimination without an experimentally derived RNA conformational ensemble. Prospective screening against IRES-derived RNA hairpins from cMyc and XIAP mRNAs further identifies multiple experimentally validated, micromolar-affinity binders from a diverse chemical library. These results demonstrate that SIREN generalizes to unseen RNA targets, transfers across independent benchmarks, and provides a scalable, structure-free framework for RNA-targeted compound prioritization that complements existing structure-based screening approaches.

papers.title: Deep learning design and in vivo validation of Müller glia-specific cis-regulatory elements
papers.abstract: Effective recombinant adeno-associated virus gene therapies require promoters that are compact and cell-type-specific. Ideally, promoters should also exhibit functional conservation when tested in model organisms to ensure that preclinical findings translate reliably to human patients. Here, we introduce a deep learning framework for designing cis-regulatory elements (CREs) meeting these criteria, applied to retinal Muller glia (MG). Using single-cell chromatin accessibility data from human and mouse retinas, we trained species-specific models to predict cell-type accessibility, and designed compact CREs using two complementary strategies. In silico validation predicted that the designed CREs exhibit high MG-specific accessibility (on-target) in both species with minimal off-target accessibility across hundreds of human cell types and tissues. Mechanistic analysis revealed that the predicted MG accessibility is driven by the creation of LHX2 motifs. In vivo validation confirmed that the designed CREs successfully restrict reporter expression to MG in the murine retina. Our deep learning framework is highly generalizable and enables the rapid design of compact, on-target, and species-conserved CREs for precision gene therapy.

papers.title: PedDx: An End-to-End Deep Learning Framework for Pediatric Posterior Fossa Tumor Diagnosis with Agentic AI-Enabled Independent External Evaluation
papers.abstract: Reliable clinical translation of diagnostic artificial intelligence (AI) requires evaluation beyond classification accuracy. We developed PedDx, a segmentation-free framework for pediatric posterior fossa tumor diagnosis using T2-weighted MRI, pretrained 3DINO representations, calibrated predictions, and confidence-based abstention. Evaluation included 492 discovery, 114 replication, 129 external validation, and 40 independently tested cases, alongside 236 out-of-distribution (OOD) cases and controlled imaging perturbations. Classification accuracy was 79.8% in replication and 81.4% in external validation, increasing to 90.5% and 88.7%, respectively, among non-abstained cases. OOD analyses revealed performance degradation and confidently incorrect predictions, while perturbation analyses identified acquisition and alignment vulnerabilities. An external institution independently executed the complete agentic workflow, successfully generating predictions and structured quality-control reports for all 40 cases, with classification accuracy of 92.5%, increasing to 97.3% among non-abstained cases. PedDx demonstrates how uncertainty assessment, failure-mode characterization, external validation, and independently reproducible, traceable reporting can collectively inform the reliability and limitations of diagnostic AI systems.

papers.title: scDiffusion: conditional generation of high-quality single-cell data using diffusion model
papers.abstract: MOTIVATION: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data are important for studying the laws of life at single-cell level. However, it is still challenging to obtain enough high-quality scRNA-seq data. To mitigate the limited availability of data, generative models have been proposed to computationally generate synthetic scRNA-seq data. Nevertheless, the data generated with current models are not very realistic yet, especially when we need to generate data with controlled conditions. In the meantime, diffusion models have shown their power in generating data with high fidelity, providing a new opportunity for scRNA-seq generation. RESULTS: In this study, we developed scDiffusion, a generative model combining the diffusion model and foundation model to generate high-quality scRNA-seq data with controlled conditions. We designed multiple classifiers to guide the diffusion process simultaneously, enabling scDiffusion to generate data under multiple condition combinations. We also proposed a new control strategy called Gradient Interpolation. This strategy allows the model to generate continuous trajectories of cell development from a given cell state. Experiments showed that scDiffusion could generate single-cell gene expression data closely resembling real scRNA-seq data. Also, scDiffusion can conditionally produce data on specific cell types including rare cell types. Furthermore, we could use the multiple-condition generation of scDiffusion to generate cell type that was out of the training data. Leveraging the Gradient Interpolation strategy, we generated a continuous developmental trajectory of mouse embryonic cells. These experiments demonstrate that scDiffusion is a powerful tool for augmenting the real scRNA-seq data and can provide insights into cell fate research. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: scDiffusion is openly available at the GitHub repository https://github.com/EperLuo/scDiffusion or Zenodo https://zenodo.org/doi/10.5281/zenodo.13268742.

papers.title: Molecular Characterization of T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia by an Optimal-Transport Based Multi-Omics Integration Framework
papers.abstract: T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL) is an aggressive pediatric malignancy characterized by complex heterogeneity across multiple molecular layers. Accurate subtyping is essential for understanding disease mechanisms, risk stratification, and guiding targeted therapeutic strategies. However, current diagnostic approaches are labor-intensive and time-consuming, and existing computational methods are limited by reliance on single-modality data or simple integration strategies. Effective integration of heterogeneous multi-omics data remains a major computational challenge. We present OTTER (Optimal Transport-based Transcriptomics and gEnomics Representation), a novel multi-modal deep learning framework that jointly models transcriptomic and genomic data for T-ALL molecular characterization. OTTER encodes each omics modality through a modality-specific encoder and aligns the resulting latent representations using Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport (GW-OT), which preserves the internal geometric structure of each modality without requiring a shared feature space. Benchmarking tests on the Children's Oncology Group (COG) AALL0434 cohort with >1,300 patients across 17 T-ALL subtypes suggested that OTTER significantly outperformed state-of-the-art approaches for T-ALL molecular characterization. In addition, OTTER could identify interpretable subtype-defining and omics-specific features for T-ALL. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the generalizability of OTTER by evaluating on multiple external independent clinical cohorts. In summary, OTTER provides a principled, biologically interpretable, and computationally effective framework for multi-omics driven T-ALL molecular characterization and broader cancer applications.

papers.title: Regional Signals Matter: Rethinking Global Pooling for mRNA Foundation Models
papers.abstract: RNA foundation models with diverse architectures have shown promise for learning representations of messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences. However, existing benchmarks commonly reduce token-level embeddings to transcript-level representations through global mean pooling before fitting a downstream probe. This aggregation does not explicitly preserve the identities of biologically distinct mRNA regions. Consequently, signals associated with short regulatory regions may be diluted, confounding assessments of representation quality with the information preserved by the readout. We introduce an architecture-agnostic, region-aware readout that separately averages embeddings within the 5$'$ untranslated region (UTR), coding sequence, and 3$'$ UTR and concatenates the resulting representations for linear probing. We reproduce mRNABench evaluations for 20 frozen models from 18 families, with a median absolute score difference of 0.0009 across 380 model--dataset--target evaluations published for 19 models, and construct a region-aware benchmark using the same models, tasks, and splits. Relative to global mean pooling, region-aware pooling increases Pearson correlation, averaged across the 20 models, by 11--25\% on translation and stability tasks, with no statistically significant decreases detected for any model on the regression tasks. On classification tasks, relative changes in the area under the precision--recall curve range from $-3\%$ to $+11\%$. Boundary randomization and displacement generally reduce performance, while dimensionality-matched and sequence-composition controls indicate that the gains are not explained solely by increased feature dimensionality, region length, or guanine--cytosine (GC) content. Learned attention pooling approaches region-aware performance only when supplied with one query per region. In silico perturbations reveal stronger sensitivity to upstream AUGs (uAUGs) and their Kozak context, while analyses of endogenous transcripts show approximately threefold greater recovery of length- and GC-adjusted uAUG-associated differences than global-mean probes. Both readouts capture codon optimality. Model rankings averaged over the regression tasks remain largely stable, while within a task models move by several places. Our region-aware benchmark therefore provides a biologically structured and complementary evaluation of mRNA foundation models, revealing regulatory information that is less accessible to linear probes after global mean pooling. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/Sanford-Labs/rnaregionpooling

papers.title: Protein Language Models Fail To Capture Contact Predictions Under Invariant Relabeling
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) produce highly accurate contact maps from single-sequence inputs. People often take this accuracy as proof that these models implicitly learn invariant coevolutionary statistics, extracting the same signals as classical alignment-based methods like Potts. In this work, we introduce a diagnostic framework around a global bijective relabeling of the amino-acid alphabet. This transformation permutes residue letters while leaving all alignment-level information, column entropies, and pairwise edit distances unchanged. Pseudolikelihood Potts models and inverse-covariance estimators remain invariant under this transformation, but pLMs fail the test. Across multiple architectures (ESM-2, MSA Transformer, AMPLIFY) and model scales (8M to 3B parameters), pLM contact maps collapse under arbitrary relabeling. Using Hamming distance controls and biochemical grouping interventions, we attempt to isolate what likely causes this degradation and find that these models rely on explicit, canonical residue identities (``alphabet anchoring'') rather than pure coevolutionary statistics. Increasing scale makes models more responsive to biochemical classes, but their performance still degrades under relabeling. Our findings show a gap between how pLMs and classical coevolutionary models compute contacts. More broadly, our work shows how diagnostic perturbations that leave classical models provably unchanged can expose hidden representation biases and prevent over-reliance on neural black boxes in biological modeling.

papers.title: Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC.
papers.abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies measure multiple molecular layers within intact tissues. Two central challenges are vertical integration, which combines different molecular modalities, and horizontal integration, which aligns cell types across studies. Here we show domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration (DIRAC), a geometric deep learning model that unifies these tasks in a generalized domain adaptation framework. DIRAC learns task-discriminative features that are insensitive to domain shifts caused by batch effects, omic modalities or study sites, enabling a shared embedding space and automated cell-type annotation through label transfer from reference datasets. Across sequencing-based and imaging-based datasets, DIRAC identified a new microvascular proliferation domain in glioblastoma, corrected cortical-layer annotations in severe Alzheimer's disease, resolved subtle structures in mouse embryos and remained robust to missing data and unseen cell types. We generated mouse spleen and thymus Stereo-CITE-seq data and used DIRAC to reveal thymic T cell migration and splenic immune cell interactions. DIRAC is fast and scales to millions of cells.

papers.title: PmiREN3.0: a multi-omics integrated and AI-assisted encyclopedia for plant microRNA research.
papers.abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators in gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Comprehensive research on miRNAs increasingly requires the integration of large and heterogeneous datasets, together with more efficient approaches to knowledge exploration. Here, we present PmiREN3.0, a major update of the Plant MicroRNA Encyclopedia. Compared with PmiREN2.0, species/subspecies coverage increased from 179 to 340, adding 22 orders, 51 families, and 108 genera. Using the same standardized workflow and annotation criteria as previous releases, high-confidence miRNAs were identified from 5319 small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets, with miRNA loci increasing from 39 751 to 87 667 and miRNA families from 7838 to 18 389. Resources and tools from previous releases were extensively updated, while six new modules were added for primary transcripts, DNA methylation, RNA modifications, stress-responsive expression, metabolic pathways, and core GRNs. PmiREN3.0 also introduces miRai+, a knowledge service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines a language model fine-tuned on miRNA knowledge with retrieval augmented generation. Evaluation yielded scores of 0.910 for answer relevance, 0.965 for faithfulness, and 0.906 for factual correctness. Together, PmiREN3.0 provides an expanded plant miRNA dataset and an integrated platform combining multi-omics data and AI-assisted knowledge services for plant miRNA research. PmiREN3.0 is available at https://pmiren.com/.

papers.title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

papers.title: TMCells: A topic-based probabilistic framework for interpretable metacell construction in single-cell data.
papers.abstract: Metacells have emerged as an important analytical strategy for addressing the computational barriers posed by the scale and complexity of large-scale single-cell omics data, while preserving biologically relevant information and improving analytical interpretability. However, existing metacell inference methods usually have limited biological interpretability, rely on deterministic assignments that insufficiently capture continuous state transitions, and may lose potential biological signals due to prior feature selection or dimensionality reduction. We propose TMCells, an interpretable metacell identification algorithm based on a probabilistic generative framework. TMCells introduces the concept of topic modeling and uses a Gaussian mixture model as the prior for topic distribution, defining metacells as statistical distribution centers in the latent topic space. By modeling the cell generation process, TMCells enables the simultaneous learning of topic representations and metacell partitions in an end-to-end manner, capturing the continuity and uncertainty in cell state transitions. TMCells effectively identifies high-quality metacells, eliminating technical noise while preserving the original biological heterogeneity, thereby enhancing downstream analyses such as differential expression, rare cell type identification, and trajectory inference. Furthermore, TMCells provides an intuitive interpretation of cellular heterogeneity through latent topics associated with biologically meaningful regulatory programs, offering a generative perspective for dissecting regulatory dynamics during cell-state transitions. The TMCells along with detailed documentation is freely available at https://github.com/Jinsl-lab/TMCells with DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.24198840. Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: S-PLM-TM enables fast and accurate sequence-based search for remote homologs
papers.abstract: Protein structures and functions can remain conserved after extensive sequence divergence, but detecting these distant relationships across large databases remains challenging. Here we present S-PLM-TM, a sequence-only remote homology search tool based on a structure-aware protein language model. Cross-modal flow matching and contrastive learning incorporate structural information into sequence representations. A lightweight calibration head enables structural-similarity search with the frozen encoder, while a residue-level alignment head generates structural alignments directly from sequence. S-PLM-TM outperforms the tested sequence-based methods in remote homology detection, rivals structure-based methods in structural classification and retrieves the most functionally consistent neighbors. It also retrieves distantly related enzymes with shared catalytic functions at a level comparable to the best-performing structure-based methods. In large-scale database search, S-PLM-TM achieves the highest average precision among both sequence-based and alignment-free methods, with speed approaching the fastest sequence-alignment tools. Together, these results establish S-PLM-TM as a practical tool that combines sensitive and biologically informative remote homology search with the speed required for database-scale retrieval.

papers.title: CIRCA learns identifiable cell- and niche-level programs and their interactions with tissue pathology from spatial transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Interactions among cells and their local microenvironments shape tissue organization and function, while their dysregulation can contribute to disease. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), the complex responses of glial cells and neurons to amyloid-{beta} pathology can both mitigate and exacerbate neuronal injury. Spatial transcriptomics enables investigation of these relationships in situ, but recovering interpretable transcriptional programs and their interactions from spatial transcriptomics remains challenging, in part because conventional nonlinear models are non-identifiable. Here we present CIRCA (Causal Interaction Representation for Cellular Architectures), a self-supervised causal representation learning framework that jointly learns identifiable cell- and neighborhood-level transcriptional programs and the directed interactions among them under explicit assumptions. It can also be extended to incorporate additional modalities such as pathology. Benchmarked against five existing methods across seven cell-resolution datasets, CIRCA achieved the highest biological accuracy in six and the highest overall score in all five multi-section datasets, while recovering higher-order anatomical organization. In an AD mouse model, incorporating amyloid-{beta} pathology revealed four region-specific plaque niches enriched for microglia. Plaque-associated microglia shared a core disease-associated response whose strength varied by region, and AD genetic risk was preferentially enriched in hippocampal and cortical plaque-associated microglia. Reproducible latent factors linked to cell-level amyloid burden separated phagocytic from inflammatory microglial programs. Applied to a human colorectal cancer dataset, CIRCA resolved patient-specific tumor niches, conserved stromal remodeling niches, and distinct macrophage states, highlighting its versatility. Together, these results establish CIRCA as a methodological advance over existing approaches, enabling deeper insights into tissue organization and the molecular dependencies linking cells to their local environments.

papers.title: OCCAM: Improved Single-Cell Representation Learning and Perturbation Effect Prediction
papers.abstract: Predicting the effects of genetic perturbations requires models that generalize beyond observed cell contexts and gene combinations. We introduce Occam, a multilayer perceptron (MLP) framework for representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction. Occam combines cell representations learned through denoising with gene interaction, text, and protein-sequence features. It achieves the highest aggregate representation scores for perturbation information and cell-type preservation with batch integration. In cross-context few-shot prediction, a perturbation and a cell context are each observed during training, but never together. Occam better captures the measured response patterns for these unobserved combinations than four retrained competitors or direct transfer of the same perturbation's measured effects from other training cell lines. Without fine-tuning, Occam best distinguishes perturbations among the evaluated models and simple baselines in cell lines held out from predictor training, across seen and unseen assays. Predicting expression levels accurately in these settings remains challenging. For double perturbations, which target two genes simultaneously, Occam composes learned single-gene responses to better capture the combined response and reduce expression error compared with competing models and summed single-gene effects. These gains extend to both strongly additive and weakly additive responses. Together, these results support simple MLPs for cell representation learning and perturbation-effect prediction across contexts and gene combinations.

papers.title: Measuring the information budget of cross-target antibody affinity generalization: a robust cross-target wall, and why structure reaches developability but not affinity
papers.abstract: Structure-based machine learning is widely expected to advance antibody engineering, yet it is unclear how far affinity predictions transfer to new targets, and why. We introduce a noise-corrected, censoring-aware estimator of the cross-target transfer ceiling, {rho}max = {surd}(T/(T+I)), which separates a transferable antibody-intrinsic component (T) from a non-transferable target-specific interaction (I). On deterministic synthetic ground truth the estimator recovers the noise-free ceiling to {+/-} 0.0003, whereas the naive sum-of-squares estimator is biased downward by measurement noise. Applying it from synthetic to real systems, the transferable budget is small, and on real neutralization panels it is not an artefact: the target-specific interaction survives noise and censoring correction. It is strongly regime-dependent, with a two-tier structure: predicting a novel antibody from sequence alone (the design setting) reaches a lower ceiling ({rho} {approx} 0.44 on real breadth data) than ranking a characterized one ({rho} {approx} 0.59), even with a strong protein language model. Synthetic oracles also overstate transferability: an oracle scored on real predicted structures carries about half the budget of a matched synthetic lattice (0.45 vs. 0.81), and real neutralization and escape panels sit well below the synthetic ceiling (0.32-0.68).
