With application to five in vitro and in vivo spatial datasets, we show that CCST outperforms other spatial cluster approaches on spatial transcriptomics datasets, and can clearly identify all four cell cycle phases from MERFISH data of cultured cells, and find novel functional sub cell types with different micro-environments from seqFISH+ data of brain, which are all validated experimentally, inspiring novel biological hypotheses about the underlying interactions among cell state, cell type and micro-environment.

papers.title: YAP1-induced super-enhancer rewiring mediates gene-environment-driven malignant reprogramming and metastatic ecosystem formation in head and neck cancer
papers.abstract: Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) is characterized by frequent TP53 mutations, which are insufficient for tumorigenesis and largely undruggable, underscoring the need to define epigenetic mechanisms driving cancer evolution. Here we show that TP53 mutation facilitates YAP1-dependent transcriptional reprogramming, driving epigenetic tumor evolution by hijacking tissue-regenerative programs. Integrated multi-omics analyses of mouse models and multiregional human HNSCC samples reveal that global chromatin architecture remains largely stable during progression, whereas YAP1 dynamically redistributes to newly formed super-enhancers accompanied by enhancer DNA hypomethylation. Mechanistically, YAP1 establishes an IL6-dependent feedforward loop and cooperates with stage-specific transcription factors, including FOXM1, DeltaNp63, and PITX2. The YAP1-PITX2 axis promotes partial EMT, cancer-associated fibroblast activation, and lymph node metastasis, resulting in a fibrotic and immunosuppressive metastatic ecosystem. These findings identify a YAP1-driven epigenetic circuit as a central hub linking environmental stress to malignant reprogramming and highlight a potential therapeutic vulnerability in HNSCC.

papers.title: SpaAxFormer: Fine-Grained Token Modeling of Spatial Transcriptomics with Axial Transformers
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics combines gene-expression measurements with spatial relationships between cells. We investigate how spatial context can be incorporated into gene-resolved representations while preserving explicit input-gene correspondence. SpaAxFormer is a spatially constrained factorized formulation that maintains contextual cell-gene states throughout the encoder. It first contextualizes genes within each cell and then exchanges corresponding gene states across spatial neighbors, while a separate CLS representation provides a cell-level summary. Contextual gene states support gene-expression reconstruction, while CLS-conditioned reconstruction and contrastive learning provide complementary supervision for the cell-level representation. We evaluate SpaAxFormer on gene-expression imputation and spatial-domain identification across multiple spatial-transcriptomics technologies. Compared with the included baselines, imputation results were most favorable on dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) datasets and more mixed on additional technologies, while post-hoc spatial refinement consistently improved mean ARI on the Visium spatial-domain datasets where it was applied. In a single-slice component-addition analysis, mean clustering ARI increased as CLS-conditioned reconstruction and contrastive supervision were added. Together, these results show that the same gene-resolved formulation can support complementary gene-level prediction and cell-level spatial representation while preserving explicit input-gene correspondence.

papers.title: SubCellSeg: A generalist model for subcellular structure segmentation in 3D fluorescence microscopy
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) segmentation of subcellular structures from fluorescence microscopy images is the foundation of many analyses in quantitative cell biology. The prevailing approach addresses 3D segmentation one structure at a time, with a separate model trained for each structure type. By developing SubCellSeg, we demonstrate that a single model, trained jointly across a diverse range of structures, substantially and consistently outperforms structure-specific specialist models. SubCellSeg is a 3D segmentation model trained on expert-curated fluorescence images and their computationally generated reference masks, of 13 morphologically distinct subcellular structures in human induced pluripotent stem (hiPS) cell lines from the Allen Cell Collection, spanning compact puncta, planar junctions, reticular networks, and tubular structures. Without any structure-specific input, SubCellSeg achieves a mean Dice score of 0.909 across the 13 structures and outperforms each of the 13 specialist models on the structure it was trained for (specialist mean Dice 0.773). SubCellSeg also achieves zero-shot generalization, segmenting subcellular structures with morphologies not represented in the training data. This generalization extends to images acquired on different microscopes and with different imaging configurations, to cells under drug perturbation, and to a morphologically distinct cell type, hiPS cell-derived cardiomyocytes. Where zero-shot results are insufficient for a specific application, SubCellSeg can be fine-tuned: starting from its pretrained weights, 10% of the labeled images (16 images) gave better results than training a new model from scratch on all of them. SubCellSeg is distributed through the napari plugin allencell-segmenter-ml[1] with pretrained checkpoints, so it can be run on new data without any training; the training and evaluation code is available at https://github.com/AllenCell/SubCellSeg.

papers.title: The Confessions of a Protein Language Model: Steering, Activations, and What Predicted Confidence Cannot Certify
papers.abstract: Protein generate-and-screen pipelines use interventions and readouts to select candidates, but rarely test whether these track their intended targets. We audit published repetition steering, ESMFold confidence, and an activation readout. Steering preserves confidence at its operating point, but a fitted cliff follows at alpha_50 = 1.240x (sweep's own control: 64.0%). Direction matters at moderate matched-norm push, but not at saturation. Unsteered generator activations predict the confidence gate (ROC-AUC 0.786 +/- 0.004), supporting cost-aware, model-specific triage. We also replicate established length sensitivity, through which shortening can manufacture false nulls. Yet on composition- and length-matched design--scramble pairs, no balanced-accuracy interval excludes chance for experimental stability. Predicting the gate does not establish foldability. We should test what a readout measures before using it to select. Code and data: https://github.com/paninishah/plm-steering-audit

papers.title: REVEAL: RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes
papers.abstract: Capturing the sparsely populated but functionally important, excited states of RNA remains a central challenge for molecular simulation, because the underlying transitions are rare events that unbiased molecular dynamics cannot reach from a single starting structure. Here we introduce REVEAL (RNA Ensemble Validation and Exploration with AI-guided Landscapes), a workflow that couples generative secondary structure sampling, secondary structure conditioned tertiary structure prediction with trRosettaRNA2, unbiased molecular dynamics and Markov state modeling. Using only the sequence of the engineered HIV-1 TAR mutant, in which the excited state ES2 is the dominant conformation, we show that REVEAL captures the reversible ES2 to GS register shift from 6.8 s of aggregate unbiased sampling across 34 seeds, recovering both basins, the intermediate states, and correctly identifies ES2 as the dominant state, consistent with the design of the construct. In contrast, molecular dynamics seeded from the ES2-dominant HIV-1 TAR mutant NMR ensemble remains trapped in ES2 despite substantially longer aggregate simulation time, and sequence-only ensemble predictors (AlphaFold3, Boltz-2, ESMFold2, OpenFold3 and Protenix-v2) place every structure near the ground state and invert the experimentally observed population ordering. The information content of the seed ensemble, rather than the total simulation time, determines whether the transition is sampled. We further introduce ''population-weighted consensus score'' (PWCS) that ranks conformers by how representative they are of the equilibrium ensemble directly from the simulation data, without experimental restraints and independent of the choice of collective variables. PWCS identifies the dominant state even when low-dimensional representations fail to separate the states. Built entirely from open-source tools, REVEAL provides a transparent and extensible route to RNA conformational ensembles beyond the single-structure paradigm.

papers.title: Spatial transcriptomics prediction from histology jointly through Transformer and graph neural networks
papers.abstract: The rapid development of spatial transcriptomics allows the measurement of RNA abundance at a high spatial resolution, making it possible to simultaneously profile gene expression, spatial locations of cells or spots, and the corresponding hematoxylin and eosin-stained histology images. It turns promising to predict gene expression from histology images that are relatively easy and cheap to obtain. For this purpose, several methods are devised, but they have not fully captured the internal relations of the 2D vision features or spatial dependency between spots. Here, we developed Hist2ST, a deep learning-based model to predict RNA-seq expression from histology images. Around each sequenced spot, the corresponding histology image is cropped into an image patch and fed into a convolutional module to extract 2D vision features. Meanwhile, the spatial relations with the whole image and neighbored patches are captured through Transformer and graph neural network modules, respectively. These learned features are then used to predict the gene expression by following the zero-inflated negative binomial distribution. To alleviate the impact by the small spatial transcriptomics data, a self-distillation mechanism is employed for efficient learning of the model. By comprehensive tests on cancer and normal datasets, Hist2ST was shown to outperform existing methods in terms of both gene expression prediction and spatial region identification. Further pathway analyses indicated that our model could reserve biological information. Thus, Hist2ST enables generating spatial transcriptomics data from histology images for elucidating molecular signatures of tissues.

papers.title: MicrobeRT: A Framework and Suite of Fine-tuned Language Models for Genomic Sequences
papers.abstract: Accurate and reproducible metagenomic analysis is essential for effective infectious disease surveillance. Targeted diagnostics such as culturing, antigen assays, and multiplex PCR panels identify only predefined organisms and can fail to identify atypical or novel infections. Shotgun metagenomics offers hypothesis-free detection, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity, dependence on mutable reference databases, and high computational cost. To combat these challenges, we introduce MicrobeRT, an integrated suite of genomic language models fine-tuned to classify metagenomic sequencing reads across three tasks: (i) species level taxonomic identification, (ii) antibiotic resistance gene detection, and (iii) pathogenicity assessment. The framework builds on three pre-trained genomic language models - Nucleotide Transformer (Dalla-Torre et al 2025), DNABERT (Ji et al 2021, Zhou et al 2024), and HyenaDNA (Nguyen et al 2024) - leveraging their large-scale genomic pre-training, adaptability to downstream tasks, and, in the case of HyenaDNA, ability to capture long-range sequence dependencies. The models are fine-tuned on large, curated datasets spanning microbial, viral, fungal, and human genomes, including more than 500,000 genomes and 250,000 antibiotic resistance gene sequences. To evaluate the performance of our fine-tuned genomic language models across classification tasks, we developed a benchmarking framework that compares MicrobeRT against state-of-the-art (SOTA) bioinformatics tools. Across both simulated and empirical datasets, the models achieve strong performance while reducing computational overhead. MicrobeRT is released as open-source software, enabling further fine-tuning and reproducible integration of alternative models and classifiers. We also demonstrate seamless, drop-in integration by incorporating our fine-tuned taxonomic classification models as an optional add-on within the open-source TaxTriage pipeline (Merritt et al 2026). MicrobeRT demonstrates the feasibility of three clinically relevant multi-label analyses, offering a practical path to scalable, reproducible metagenomic diagnostics and enabling broader deployment of AI/ML-enhanced infectious disease testing.

papers.title: Mind Control of LLMs via Closed-Loop Stimulation: Out-of-Distribution Robustness
papers.abstract: Brains and large language models need not be considered equivalent systems to reveal an interpretable commonality: both exhibit high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics whose behavior can only be modeled imperfectly. This creates a shared challenge whenever we seek to intervene in their dynamics. A controller may either rely on a model identified around a particular operating regime and risk failure as the system moves away from that regime, or explicitly account for uncertainty and a changing internal state. Neurostimulation has confronted an analogous problem for decades. The limitations of fixed, open-loop stimulation have motivated closed-loop and state-dependent approaches that condition intervention on the ongoing state of the neural system. Inspired by this principle, we formulate LLM steering as a feedback-control problem in which the network's internal state, rather than a fixed intervention alone, determines how the system is perturbed. We further account for the mismatch between tractable dynamical models and the nonlinear transformer they approximate through robust control. As one principled realization of this framework, we develop an $H_\infty$-based steering controller that limits sensitivity to disturbances and linearization mismatches. Across multiple steering benchmarks, the controller improves performance over existing baselines, with particularly pronounced gains under out-of-distribution conditions and varying length complexities. Beyond controller performance, we introduce robust steerability, $S_{\mathrm{rob}}$, a pre-deployment measure of tolerance to dynamics mismatch; across model-task pairs, it exhibits task-specific structure and varies systematically with model scale. Beyond robust LLM steering, our measure asks not merely whether control is possible, but how much uncertainty it can survive; a principle that may span artificial and biological neural systems.

papers.title: Computable Genomes: A Layered Computational Framework for Non-Coding DNA and Cellular Behavior
papers.abstract: Genome-wide association studies have catalogued tens of thousands of trait-associated loci, most of them in non-coding DNA, yet for most loci the path from nucleotide to phenotype remains correlational. We propose a layered computational decomposition of the genome as a complement to data-driven approaches: sequence as formal language, sequence as information-bearing signal, mobile elements as runtime, compilation to interaction networks through thermodynamic and rule-based models, and execution as cellular and multicellular dynamics. Each layer is defined by its inputs, outputs and formalisms, and we set out where the frame breaks down, including the looseness of algorithmic-information estimates, the triviality of universality results and the failure of string grammars at the chromatin level. Synthetic-biology platforms serve as tests of whether the layers compose, and genomic foundation models and the AlphaGenome Atlas, which predicts effects for all nine billion possible single-nucleotide variants, serve as oracles whose coverage and limits we map onto the framework. We state five falsifiable predictions and test the first, that sequence compressibility carries information about regulatory function beyond composition and conservation, on 38,556 single-nucleotide variants from a saturation-mutagenesis reporter assay of 21 regulatory elements. In a pooled model, local compressibility is associated with measured effect size (standardized {beta} = -0.030, p = 0.0014). The association roughly halves under full control for base composition, loses significance when composition, motif and noise adjustments are combined under locus-level inference (wild cluster bootstrap p = 0.11), and averages zero within loci (random-effects {beta} = -0.0003, p = 0.90). The prediction is therefore not supported at the variant level in these data, which bound the effect a genome-wide test should expect. The argument is not that the genome "is" a program, but that treating it as one supplies formal tools whose predictions can be checked.

papers.title: Constructing Gene Regulatory Network using Chatterjee's Rank Correlation with Single-cell Transcriptomic Data
papers.abstract: Constructing gene regulatory networks (GRNs) from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data is critical for understanding cellular systems, yet existing methods rely either on strong modeling assumptions or on computationally intensive algorithms. We introduce a multiple testing framework for GRN construction based on Chatterjee's rank correlation coefficient, a nonparametric measure of dependence that captures non-linear and non-monotone relationships. The framework overcomes several limitations of traditional methods by offering a transparent, scalable, and computationally efficient alternative to recent black-box machine learning models. Because cells in scRNA-seq data are not independent observations, we develop a data-driven algorithm for estimating robust testing cutoffs. We further exploit the asymmetric nature of Chatterjee's correlation to propose a new test for asymmetric predictive associations, yielding biologically meaningful and directionally informed GRNs. In simulations, our method matches or outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in recovering true gene-gene dependencies and asymmetric associations, particularly for complex, non-linear dependencies. Application to real scRNA-seq data shows its utility for dissecting complex regulatory networks.

papers.title: Automated segmentation of renal structures using brightfield images of unstained kidney biopsies
papers.abstract: The automated segmentation of unstained kidney brightfield microscopy images remains a significant challenge in medical imaging. In conventional histopathology, staining provides crucial structural and molecular contrast, allowing renal compartments and structures to be readily distinguished. The absence of staining markedly reduces this contrast, obscuring the fine architectural details that are essential for diagnosis. Addressing this gap would reduce reliance on staining protocols, reduce technical and interpretive variability, and preserve valuable tissue for downstream molecular or multi-omics analyses. Ultimately, automation of unstained image segmentation could enable faster, more objective tissue analysis while preserving samples for further molecular testing. In this work, we provide a comprehensive review of state-of-the-art segmentation methods applied to renal brightfield microscopy images. Current findings highlight a predominance of Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) based architectures for semantic segmentation approaches while recent trends point to the growing application of transformer-based and instance-segmentation strategies. However, the field is still hampered by the scarcity and poor annotation of publicly available renal datasets. Aiming to further contribute to the enhancement of the field, a dataset of 18 Whole Slide Images (WSIs) of unstained human kidney tissue is made publicly available. Additionally, in the dataset, we provide 543 annotated tiles extracted from the WSIs, facilitating further research into stain-independent segmentation approaches. As a third contribution, we present a preliminary case study, evaluating state-of-the-art deep learning segmentation architectures, including U-Net and Segment Anything Model (SAM). Our preliminary results indicate that deep learning models demonstrate promising segmentation performance in unstained kidney biopsies. In alignment with these findings, advanced customised loss functions and data augmentation were integrated into the supervised training of the promising U-Net, DeepLabv3+, and TransUNet models, achieving significant improvements compared to the baseline experiments. To exploit the abundance of unlabelled data, we further tested FixMatchSeg, a semi-supervised learning method; however, its segmentation performance remained slightly behind the supervised methods. Taken together, these contributions establish a foundation for future research in stain-independent Computational Pathology, demonstrating that unstained brightfield microscopy images can reliably support downstream tissue analysis tasks. Our dataset, validation experiments, and methodological insights provide the community with both resources and benchmarks to advance robust, data-efficient, and generalisable kidney tissue segmentation.

papers.title: GRABS: a content-addressed antibody-antigen binding-affinity dataset with predicted structures and a leak-free benchmark
papers.abstract: Machine-learning prediction of antibody-antigen binding affinity depends as much on the training data as on the model, yet public affinity measurements are scattered across databases with incompatible formats, mix genuine dissociation constants with censored or predicted values, and concentrate most of their label mass on a few heavily mutated targets. We present GRABS (Geometric Resource for Antibody Binding Studies), a curated, content-addressed, structure-ready dataset that consolidates nine public sources, of which the seven with redistributable licenses yield 4,380 canonical antibody-antigen records} (median-collapsed from 4,761 raw measurements), each with an experimentally measured dissociation constant (Kd), paired heavy and light variable regions (VH, VL), and an antigen sequence, covering 2,015 distinct antigen sequences. Every structure, graph, and feature is addressed by a content key, md5(VH+VL+antigen)[:10], and verified non-circularly: each graph's node features are decoded back to sequence and re-hashed, matching the content key for 4,282/4,282 (100%) structure-backed records. This integrity is load-bearing: an alignment ablation shows that a previously-reported strong cross-target result (R2 {approx} 0.415) was a misalignment-mediated source/batch leak that content-key regeneration dissolves. On the resulting leak-free, antigen-cluster-grouped benchmark, cross-target ranking of variants of a held-out antigen collapses to the noise floor (within-held-out-antigen Spearman {rho} {approx} 0 for every model family: sequence, structure, and folding-confidence), with structure giving no advantage, a rigorously leakage-controlled quantification of the limited reach of current methods. GRABS ships model-ready artifacts (Boltz-2 predicted complexes, per-residue ESM-2 embeddings, geometric graphs, feature vectors) with antigen-stratified splits, and is intended for leakage-free benchmarking and within-target affinity ranking (measure-then-rank), not zero-shot prediction for antigens absent from training.

papers.title: Metabolic transitions reprogram translation through sequence-dependent regulation
papers.abstract: Cells suppress protein synthesis during starvation, but how translation recovers upon nutrient repletion remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we followed translational recovery in budding yeast after repletion of glucose, nitrogen, or phosphate, combining time-resolved metabolomics, structural proteomics, transcriptomics, and spike-in-calibrated ribosome profiling. Nutrient addition rapidly altered ribosome occupancy in distinct, transcript-specific programs. To identify their sequence determinants, we developed RiboNet, a deep learning framework that predicts ribosome load and positions along transcripts from mRNA sequence. RiboNet-guided in silico mutagenesis revealed reduced pausing at serine codons upon glucose repletion and transiently increased pausing at leucine codons following nitrogen repletion. These responses coincided with altered cognate tRNA charging and metabolite-associated structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. RiboNet also identified a conserved 5' UTR motif, GAUY, that increased reporter protein output following glucose repletion. Our findings reveal how metabolic state alters the contributions of mRNA sequence features to translation initiation and elongation.

papers.title: A benchmark study of deep learning-based multi-omics data fusion methods for cancer
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: A fused method using a combination of multi-omics data enables a comprehensive study of complex biological processes and highlights the interrelationship of relevant biomolecules and their functions. Driven by high-throughput sequencing technologies, several promising deep learning methods have been proposed for fusing multi-omics data generated from a large number of samples. RESULTS: In this study, 16 representative deep learning methods are comprehensively evaluated on simulated, single-cell, and cancer multi-omics datasets. For each of the datasets, two tasks are designed: classification and clustering. The classification performance is evaluated by using three benchmarking metrics including accuracy, F1 macro, and F1 weighted. Meanwhile, the clustering performance is evaluated by using four benchmarking metrics including the Jaccard index (JI), C-index, silhouette score, and Davies Bouldin score. For the cancer multi-omics datasets, the methods' strength in capturing the association of multi-omics dimensionality reduction results with survival and clinical annotations is further evaluated. The benchmarking results indicate that moGAT achieves the best classification performance. Meanwhile, efmmdVAE, efVAE, and lfmmdVAE show the most promising performance across all complementary contexts in clustering tasks. CONCLUSIONS: Our benchmarking results not only provide a reference for biomedical researchers to choose appropriate deep learning-based multi-omics data fusion methods, but also suggest the future directions for the development of more effective multi-omics data fusion methods. The deep learning frameworks are available at https://github.com/zhenglinyi/DL-mo .

papers.title: FLASH radiotherapy drives intestinal regeneration via macrophage-derived WNT4 signaling and attenuated T-cell inflammation
papers.abstract: Ultra-high dose rate radiotherapy (FLASH-RT) reduces normal-tissue toxicity, yet how elevated dose rate improves tissue repair remains unclear. Here we combined whole-abdominal FLASH-RT and conventional radiotherapy (CONV-RT) in mice with single-cell transcriptomics, trajectory analysis, cell-cell communication inference, and in vivo perturbation experiments to define the intestinal repair ecosystem. Compared with CONV-RT, FLASH preserved Lgr5+ intestinal stem cells and Fabp1+ absorptive epithelial cells. Trajectory analysis showed that FLASH maintained stem-cell differentiation toward mature epithelial states enriched for fatty-acid metabolism. During a day-3 repair window, FLASH was accompanied by enrichment of Mrc1 macrophages, increased WNT4-associated signaling involving Fzd5Lrp5/6-expressing stem cells, and early transient {beta}-catenin activation. In vivo augmentation of Wnt4 signaling promoted crypt regeneration after CONV-RT. FLASH also reduced Tcf7 and Tbx21 CD4 T-cell populations and TNF- levels, consistent with attenuation of the pro-inflammatory CD4 T-cell response during intestinal recovery. Together, these findings indicate that FLASH-associated tissue sparing involves coordinated remodeling of regenerative and inflammatory immune states, suggesting that radiation dose rate influences not only initial tissue injury but also the immune microenvironment of subsequent recovery. Targeting this immune-stem cell crosstalk may provide a strategy to mimic FLASH-like radioprotection.

papers.title: Beyond Sequence and Structure: Pretraining PLMs on Continuous Biophysical Fields
papers.abstract: We introduce the Biophysical Transformer, a protein language model that adds continuous biophysical fields as a third pretraining signal beside sequence and structure. A Poisson-Boltzmann solver computes the electrostatic potential around each three-residue token, and the model learns to predict it from sequence alone. A rotationally invariant spherical-harmonic descriptor serves as the loss target, eliminating the need for frame alignment during training and for coordinates at inference. Against a matched, one-flag control on the FLIP Meltome thermostability benchmark, the field objective raises Spearman correlation on every trained head of both human splits.The gain on human survives residualizing dipeptide composition under two architecturally different readouts and survives removing the test proteins that overlap the pretraining corpus. No effect survives on the organism-mixed split. At 1.1M parameters, both the Biophysical Transformer and its sequence-only control exceed FLIP's one-hot CNN and untrained-ESM baselines on every split. All results rest on a single pretraining run per arm,and the current design does not separate field content from generic regularization.

papers.title: A mixture-of-experts deep generative model for integrated analysis of single-cell multiomics data
papers.abstract: The recent development of single-cell multiomics analysis has enabled simultaneous detection of multiple traits at the single-cell level, providing deeper insights into cellular phenotypes and functions in diverse tissues. However, currently, it is challenging to infer the joint representations and learn relationships among multiple modalities from complex multimodal single-cell data. Here, we present scMM, a novel deep generative model-based framework for the extraction of interpretable joint representations and crossmodal generation. scMM addresses the complexity of data by leveraging a mixture-of-experts multimodal variational autoencoder. The pseudocell generation strategy of scMM compensates for the limited interpretability of deep learning models, and the proposed approach experimentally discovered multimodal regulatory programs associated with latent dimensions. Analysis of recently produced datasets validated that scMM facilitates high-resolution clustering with rich interpretability. Furthermore, we show that crossmodal generation by scMM leads to more precise prediction and data integration compared with the state-of-the-art and conventional approaches.

papers.title: scGNN is a novel graph neural network framework for single-cell RNA-Seq analyses
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-Seq) is widely used to reveal the heterogeneity and dynamics of tissues, organisms, and complex diseases, but its analyses still suffer from multiple grand challenges, including the sequencing sparsity and complex differential patterns in gene expression. We introduce the scGNN (single-cell graph neural network) to provide a hypothesis-free deep learning framework for scRNA-Seq analyses. This framework formulates and aggregates cell-cell relationships with graph neural networks and models heterogeneous gene expression patterns using a left-truncated mixture Gaussian model. scGNN integrates three iterative multi-modal autoencoders and outperforms existing tools for gene imputation and cell clustering on four benchmark scRNA-Seq datasets. In an Alzheimer's disease study with 13,214 single nuclei from postmortem brain tissues, scGNN successfully illustrated disease-related neural development and the differential mechanism. scGNN provides an effective representation of gene expression and cell-cell relationships. It is also a powerful framework that can be applied to general scRNA-Seq analyses.

papers.title: Single-cell spatial landscapes of the lung tumour immune microenvironment
papers.abstract: Abstract Single-cell technologies have revealed the complexity of the tumour immune microenvironment with unparalleled resolution 1–9 . Most clinical strategies rely on histopathological stratification of tumour subtypes, yet the spatial context of single-cell phenotypes within these stratified subgroups is poorly understood. Here we apply imaging mass cytometry to characterize the tumour and immunological landscape of samples from 416 patients with lung adenocarcinoma across five histological patterns. We resolve more than 1.6 million cells, enabling spatial analysis of immune lineages and activation states with distinct clinical correlates, including survival. Using deep learning, we can predict with high accuracy those patients who will progress after surgery using a single 1-mm 2 tumour core, which could be informative for clinical management following surgical resection. Our dataset represents a valuable resource for the non-small cell lung cancer research community and exemplifies the utility of spatial resolution within single-cell analyses. This study also highlights how artificial intelligence can improve our understanding of microenvironmental features that underlie cancer progression and may influence future clinical practice.

papers.title: Revolutionizing Pharmaceutical Research: Harnessing Machine Learning for a Paradigm Shift in Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: The fusion of machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) is experiencing a dramatic transition in the field of pharmaceutical research and development. This study examines the several effects of machine learning (ML) on different phases of medication discovery, development, and patient care. The capability of ML to quickly process huge chemical libraries and forecast interactions with target proteins is studied, starting with compound screening and selection. The potential for fewer false positives and negatives, improved hit prediction accuracy, and ensemble technique use are underlined. The part that machine learning plays in enhancing Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, and Toxicity (ADMET) profile is then explained. ML models anticipate compound actions inside the human body by analyzing molecular structures and characteristics, improving assessments of drug safety and efficacy. The article goes into further detail about predictive modeling, highlighting how machine learning may be used to find prospective therapeutic targets and confirm their applicability. The combination of multi-omics data, deep learning, and the possibility to identify similar molecular pathways across diseases highlight the game-changing potential of machine learning in this field. The article also covers the use of ML in clinical trials, highlighting its benefits for trial planning, patient recruitment, real-time monitoring, and individualized therapy predictions. By utilizing computational analysis and quantum physics, the power of machine learning-driven de novo drug creation is examined, revealing the potential to develop new therapeutic candidates. In this article, the ethical issues surrounding AI-driven drug discovery are discussed, with a focus on the necessity of transparent data utilization, human oversight, and responsible data consumption. The report ends by predicting ML's potential for pharmaceutical R&D in the future. Accelerated drug discovery pipelines, the rise of customized medicine powered by predictive models, optimized clinical trials, and a change in medication repurposing tactics are all envisaged in this. The report emphasizes the revolutionary potential of ML in altering pharmaceutical research and development while noting obstacles in data quality, model interpretability, ethics, and interdisciplinary collaboration. It is suggested that the ethical integration of AI technologies, interdisciplinary cooperation, and regulatory modifications are essential steps to unlock the full potential of ML and AI and, ultimately, provide patients throughout the world with safer, more efficient, and individualized treatments.
papers.venue: International Journal of Multidisciplinary Sciences and Arts

papers.title: DNNGP, a deep neural network-based method for genomic prediction using multi-omics data in plants
papers.abstract: Genomic prediction is an effective way to accelerate the rate of agronomic trait improvement in plants. Traditional methods typically use linear regression models with clear assumptions; such methods are unable to capture the complex relationships between genotypes and phenotypes. Non-linear models (e.g., deep neural networks) have been proposed as a superior alternative to linear models because they can capture complex non-additive effects. Here we introduce a deep learning (DL) method, deep neural network genomic prediction (DNNGP), for integration of multi-omics data in plants. We trained DNNGP on four datasets and compared its performance with methods built with five classic models: genomic best linear unbiased prediction (GBLUP); two methods based on a machine learning (ML) framework, light gradient boosting machine (LightGBM) and support vector regression (SVR); and two methods based on a DL framework, deep learning genomic selection (DeepGS) and deep learning genome-wide association study (DLGWAS). DNNGP is novel in five ways. First, it can be applied to a variety of omics data to predict phenotypes. Second, the multilayered hierarchical structure of DNNGP dynamically learns features from raw data, avoiding overfitting and improving the convergence rate using a batch normalization layer and early stopping and rectified linear activation (rectified linear unit) functions. Third, when small datasets were used, DNNGP produced results that are competitive with results from the other five methods, showing greater prediction accuracy than the other methods when large-scale breeding data were used. Fourth, the computation time required by DNNGP was comparable with that of commonly used methods, up to 10 times faster than DeepGS. Fifth, hyperparameters can easily be batch tuned on a local machine. Compared with GBLUP, LightGBM, SVR, DeepGS and DLGWAS, DNNGP is superior to these existing widely used genomic selection (GS) methods. Moreover, DNNGP can generate robust assessments from diverse datasets, including omics data, and quickly incorporate complex and large datasets into usable models, making it a promising and practical approach for straightforward integration into existing GS platforms.

papers.title: A defence-in-depth strategy for securing AI-driven biological sequence design.
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence can design biological sequences, from proteins to whole genomes, opening opportunities for medicine and biotechnology, but the same capability can be misused. The Wübben Sandpit conference brought together experts in biology, AI, biosecurity, ethics, medicine and policy to ask how the field can capture the benefits while managing the risks. Here we set out a defence-in-depth strategy that builds safeguards into every stage, from the data used to train models, to the models themselves, to the synthesis of physical DNA. We argue that responsible governance is not a brake on progress but a precondition for it.

papers.title: Large-scale proteomic characterization reveals clinically relevant subtypes of early-stage papillary thyroid cancer for prognostic prediction.
papers.abstract: Papillary thyroid cancer (PTC) has a rising incidence. The majority are diagnosed at an early stage, albeit with a minority exhibiting aggressive tendencies. Given its generally indolent nature, controversy persists regarding the management of early-stage PTCs, particularly surgical intervention and long-term surveillance strategies. Here, we conduct a large-scale proteomic characterization of early-stage PTC based on tumor samples from 797 patients. Proteomic profiling unveils clinically relevant modules and identifies six subtypes, capturing the spectrum of heterogeneity from indolent to progressive disease states. Notably, subtypes associated with higher progression risk display enhanced signatures of ribogenesis and epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Furthermore, integrating machine learning with protein co-expression network analysis, we identify predictive markers of PTC progression risk such as GPX3 and TMSB4X. Integration of clinical and proteomic data provides a valuable resource for  a deeper understanding of early-stage PTC biology and may inform personalized management strategies for patients with indolent or progressive disease.

papers.title: TFXcan reveals transcription factor programs driving GWAS loci.
papers.abstract: Disease-associated loci identified by genome-wide association studies (GWASs) may induce effects by altering transcription factor (TF) binding. However, due to the scarcity of population-level TF-binding experiments, identifying these disrupted TFs remains challenging. To address this, we present the TFXcan framework, which correlates genetically predicted TF binding with phenotypes to nominate TF-tissue pairs that may regulate complex traits. Within this framework, we introduce Enpact, a deep learning-based approach that integrates Enformer and IMPACT to infer personalized TF-binding events. Leveraging Enpact, we correlate predicted binding profiles for 700 TF-tissue pairs with prostate cancer risk, identifying multiple implicated TFs at risk loci. Matrix decomposition further reveals clusters of TF-tissue pairs, termed "programs," acting as candidate drivers of disease risk. TFXcan represents the first method capable of predicting TF binding from genotype data at scale, enabling systematic identification of TFs and regulatory programs underlying complex traits.

papers.title: Enhancing simulations of disordered protein ensembles with chemical shift restraints in coarse-grained models.
papers.abstract: With more than one third of the human proteome being structurally disordered, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) are key contributors to complex cellular functions, despite their highly dynamic conformational ensembles remaining elusive to conventional techniques in structural biology. Coarse-grained (CG) simulation methods thus serve as a gold standard to refine IDP ensembles. These methods, when relying on elastic network models or rigid body to sample secondary structure, are however inherently limited in their capability to model and sample transient secondary structure at a residue-level resolution as informed by experimental data. This fundamental limitation persists despite experimental evidence suggesting that transient structural propensities are a fundamental hallmark of IDP function. Through an artificial neural network capable of predicting backbone chemical shifts from Cα-only protein conformations, we present a generalized framework which does not rely on dihedral parameterization to equip one bead-per-aminoacid CG force fields with the ability to sample functional elements of secondary structure. When applied on a large set of IDPs in isolation or condensates, our approach correctly recapitulates both local and global arrangements, yielding experimentally informed ensembles that can inform structure-mediated function and resolve force field limitations. This can yield a fruitful exploration of ensemble-to-function relationships in IDPs, allowing to explore phenomena such as secondary structure propensity and nucleation in condensates, conformationally selected binding motifs across disordered ensembles or conformational preferences of sequence-specific short-linear motifs.
papers.venue: Proc Natl Acad Sci U S A

papers.title: Inferring single-cell gene expression profiles from multicellular spatial transcriptomics data with st2sc
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables the quantitative measurement of gene expression within tissue sections but is currently limited in spatial resolution, as each spot aggregates signals from multiple cells. Recovering single-cell gene expression profiles from these multicellular measurements requires two steps: explicit identification of individual cells and accurate estimation of per-gene expression. While existing methods have demonstrated the feasibility of recovering single-cell expression profiles, accurately estimating gene-level expression for individual cells remains an important challenge. To address this challenge, we propose st2sc (Spatial Transcriptomics to Single-Cell), an end-to-end framework for inferring single-cell gene profiles from multicellular ST data. st2sc introduces a novel Attention Gradient Flow Tracking (AGFT) algorithm that extracts attention maps from a Vision-Gene Transformer to identify candidate cell instances without predefined background constraints. The detected instances are then used by a set of regressors trained under a multiple-instance, multiple-target regression setting to predict precise single-cell gene expression counts. Comprehensive evaluations on synthetic and Visium-like datasets demonstrate that st2sc significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in accurately segmenting cellular instances and predicting gene counts. The method can further resolve contested 2um bin in Visium HD. Application to human IPF lung showed the model can recover the subtype marker level analysis. This advancement further improves single-cell resolution analysis in spatial transcriptomics, facilitating more accurate downstream biological analyses.

papers.title: Minor intron splicing restricts E2F transcription factor activity in RB-deregulated prostate cancer
papers.abstract: Castration-resistant prostate cancer with neuroendocrine differentiation (CRPC-NE) arises in RB1-mutated lineage plastic cells in response to androgen receptor (AR)-targeted therapies. RB1 loss leads to constitutive E2F activation and cylin-dependent kinase (CDK) inhibitor resistance, making it challenging to restrict E2F activity. A post-transcriptional node is that typical E2Fs contain a rare but highly conserved minor intron, processed by the minor spliceosome (MiS). In an in vivo CRISPR screen, we nominate the MiS as the strongest dependency, and U6atac correlates strongest with E2F transcriptional programs in a clinical CRPC cohort. U6atac depletion led to mis-splicing of typical E2Fs, cell cycle arrest, and translation of a minor intron-containing E2F1 isoform (E2F1-MIRI) as a pharmacodynamic biomarker. Combined E2F activator depletion, induced further neuroendocrine (NE) specification. U6atac depletion shifted NE identity along the ASCL1 axis without the secretory granule program, and induced cell-surface antigens including DLL3, nominating MiS inhibition as a combination partner for antigen-directed agents.

papers.title: Integrative analysis identifies LATS1 as a context-specific regulator of melanoma progression and immune response
papers.abstract: Malignant melanoma incidence is increasing, and survival remains poor following metastasis. The main driver oncogenes are BRAF and NRAS. Advancements in targeted agents and immunotherapies have improved survival rates, especially for patients with BRAF mutant melanoma. However, no targeted therapy options are available for patients with NRAS-mutant melanoma. Unfortunately, the development of resistance to all existing therapies remains a challenge. Recent evidence has shown that the MST2/Hippo pathway is deregulated in melanoma. The MST2 pathway core kinase LATS1 is a signalling hub that mediates the crosstalk between cell death and proliferation networks, and its inactivation has been related to melanoma progression and resistance to targeted therapy. However, the mechanisms by which LATS1 influences melanoma biology remain unclear. Here, to investigate this role of LATS1, we developed a lats1 knockout zebrafish melanoma model driven by either BRAF or NRAS mutations. Loss of Lats1 associates with reduced tumour-free survival in BRAF-mutant melanoma and a more invasive phenotype in NRAS-mutant melanoma, confirming a tumour-suppressive function. Integrating transcriptomics and proteomics datasets, we mapped molecular mechanisms mediated by Lats1 in tumours driven by these oncogenes, including pathways associated with the immune response regulated by Lats1. Subsequent validation in patient data confirmed an immune-evasive phenotype, associated with decreased LATS1 expression in BRAF-mutant melanoma. Additionally, the loss of LATS1 in NRAS mutant melanoma patients altered the expression of key DNA damage repair genes. Thus, this study identifies novel pathways controlled by LATS1 in melanoma, which aid in our understanding of the disease and offers new insights to be explored for the development of novel treatment strategies.

papers.title: Evaluating Language Models as Orchestrators in a Tool-First Biomedical Discovery Platform
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly orchestrate agentic biomedical discovery systems, but cloud deployment raises concerns about inference cost, data privacy, and governance. Small language models (SLMs) that run on-premises are an alternative, provided they orchestrate scientific tools about as well as larger models. We built a tool-first, multi-agent system for scientific discovery in which an orchestrator coordinates six specialized tool systems: differential expression, literature retrieval, pathway enrichment, network-based gene prioritization and knowledge-graph analysis, perturbation signature matching, and structural/druggability assessment. In a tool-first design, specialized tools supply the domain knowledge and computation, so the model's main task is coordination, e.g. choosing tools, passing the right parameters, calling them in the right order, and carrying results across turns. With the tools, prompts, workflow, and benchmark held constant, we compared three orchestrators, Gemma 4 (26B, open-weight and locally deployable), Gemini 2.5 Flash, and Claude Sonnet 5. Evaluation used a custom benchmark of 104 single-turn and multi-turn tests, an LLM-as-judge protocol (groundedness and evidence validity), tool-use accuracy and efficiency metrics, and blind expert review. On single-turn tasks, the three models performed comparably, and reviewers did not rate the SLM below the larger models. In multi-turn tasks, Claude Sonnet 5 showed marginally higher evidence validity, Gemma 4 was weakest when parameters had to be assembled across turns, and all three models struggled with tool ordering on memory-dependent tasks. These differences were illustrated with case studies. Finally, we propose strategies to help SLMs address the multi-turn limitations and support cost- and privacy-aware deployment.

papers.title: Gene-scale DNA and chromatin ensembles with atomic resolution
papers.abstract: The spatial organization of cellular DNA extends across a wide range of scales, from sequence-dependent base pairing to the packaging of meter-long cellular DNA into micron-size nuclei. Integrating the information from disparate experiments, molecular simulations, and theoretical models into a coherent picture of DNA and chromatin organization across scales remains challenging. Here, we introduce hierarchical chain growth for DNA (HCG-DNA) to build atomically detailed ensembles of double-stranded DNA and chromatin. Starting from complete tetranucleotide fragment libraries encoding local sequence-dependent conformations, we assemble structures of DNA up to the megabase scale at quasilinear computational cost. From HCG-DNA, the large-scale polymer elastic properties emerge, in particular the persistence length. HCG-DNA recovers electron spin resonance, atomic force microscopy, and single-molecule force spectroscopy measurements of DNA structure across scales. HCG-DNA includes nucleosomes to generate 3D atomistic chromatin ensembles constrained by cryo-electron tomography or genomic nucleosome maps. With HCG-DNA, we show how small changes in nucleosome linker length alter nucleosome packing and chromatin compaction. HCG-DNA connects atomic-level DNA and nucleosome structure to chromosome-scale spatial organization, while providing scalable ensembles for coarse-grained model development and AI training.

papers.title: CADD-SV v2.0: An Extended Framework for Structural Variant Deleteriousness Prediction Using Coordinate- and Sequence-Based Features
papers.abstract: Structural variants are a major source of genomic variation and contribute to human disease and evolution through diverse mechanisms, yet their functional interpretation remains challenging. We present CADD-SV v2.0, an improved machine learning framework for scoring SV deleteriousness that expands on the original CADD-SV implementation. This version introduces a unified Random Forest model trained on an expanded set of proxy-neutral and proxy-deleterious variants drawn from human and non-human primate genomes. The model integrates updated genomic annotations, including constraint metrics, regulatory elements, and chromatin architecture features. It scores Deletions, Insertions, Duplications and Inversions based on a single scoring framework that uses both the variant and its flanking regions. To complement this framework, we also explore sequence-based annotations derived from SegmentNT, a deep learning model that provides functional predictions from DNA sequence at nucleotide resolution. Our analysis evaluated whether sequence-derived functional signals can provide additional information for SV prioritization and whether additional models with these features alone or in combination with previous coordinate-based annotations can be used. CADD-SV v2.0 outperforms its previous version and other tools in prioritizing deleterious variants across major SV types, including some previously unsupported, and substantially improves the computational workflow, increasing predictive power for genome-wide SV interpretation.

papers.title: MINA: Do frozen DNA encoders beat sequence composition? A homology-aware linear-probe benchmark
papers.abstract: Frozen DNA encoders are widely used as feature extractors, but fine-tuning hides what their fixed embeddings already make linearly accessible. MINA is a lightweight benchmark that asks whether those embeddings beat sequence composition, with two linear probes on 3,244 human genes: 5-way classification into coarse protein families, and regression onto each gene's GenePT text-summary embedding. Mostly, they do not. On coding sequence (CDS) under a homology aware split, the validation-selected encoder, NT-v2, recovers coarse family signal at about the level of nucleotide composition (macro-F1 0.693 vs. 0.639; Holm p = 0.108) but does not reach amino-acid composition (0.767) or the protein language model ESM-2 (0.954). On GenePT, DNABERT-2 beats nucleotide composition (R2 0.065 vs. 0.039) but not amino-acid composition (0.080). Evaluation choices move scores as much as the encoder does: pooling alone takes NT-v2 from 0.504, below nucleotide composition, to 0.698; a mostly noncoding transcription-start-site window, where any signal is likely regulatory rather than family, drops NT-v2 from 0.694 to 0.300 on the same genes; and a random split inflates it from 0.693 to 0.801 through homologous genes leaking into the test set. Frozen DNA encoders thus recover little from coding sequence beyond nucleotide composition, and fair comparisons must use composition baselines and fix pooling, substrate, and split.

papers.title: Uncovering Features of ProteinMPNN with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: Customization and modification of machine learning derived sequences can be achieved by understanding the mechanics behind state-of-the-art protein design models such as ProteinMPNN. Uninterpretability is hypothesized to be due largely to polysemanticity where neural networks store more features than they have dimensions. Here, we introduce sparse autoencoders (SAEs) into ProteinMPNN which expand its latent space and uncovers correlations between the activations in sparse dimensions and the presence of protein features such as secondary structure, residue volume, residue shape, disulfide bridges, and coordination to ligands. Additionally, we show that sparse activations can be manipulated to produce a variant of the short chain variable fragment Brolucizumab that is more thermostable than variants produced by traditional machine learning methods based on high temperature molecular dynamics simulations. Thus, SAEs provide both mechanistic understanding of protein design models and allow customizable manipulation of sequence prediction.

papers.title: GENECraft: A Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System for Controllable Regulatory DNA Design
papers.abstract: Designing regulatory DNA requires reconciling two complementary modeling paradigms: genomic language models (gLMs) capture evolutionary syntax without guaranteeing targeted regulatory activity, whereas sequence-to-function predictors provide explicit functional supervision without enforcing native-like sequence plausibility. We introduce GENECraft, a training-free Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System (FP-DDS) that couples a genomic language model (Carbon) and a functional oracle (AlphaGenome) during inference-time optimization to balance predicted regulatory activity and consistency with genomic sequence priors. GENECraft evolves continuous latent nucleotide logits while evaluating strictly decoded discrete DNA sequences under a time-dependent composite vector field that fuses normalized functional utility, bidirectional contextual prior guidance, and compositional quality penalties, followed by feasibility-first trajectory readout. Across 2,185 loci spanning promoters, multi-constraint enhancers, and 18 transcription factors (TFs), GENECraft achieves full-joint success rates of 62.70%, 65.23%, and 94.56% (macro-averaged), substantially outperforming seven optimization, evolutionary, and generative baselines (which reach at most 2.15% on enhancers). In matched 336-locus ablations, in-loop Carbon guidance reduces native-relative dinucleotide divergence by 7.8--11.5%, enhancer context sensitivity by 10.5%, and TF mutation sensitivity by 11.0%, establishing FP-DDS as a principled framework for controllable regulatory DNA design.

papers.title: Fine-tuned DNA sequence language models for predicting gene expression in admixed population: A comparison with variant-based methods
papers.abstract: Predicting gene expression from whole genome sequencing data is essential for elucidating regulatory mechanisms and interpreting functional consequences of non-coding variants to complex diseases. While traditional approaches rely on variant-based linear models, DNA sequence-based language models have gained increasing popularity for their ability to learn regulatory features directly from whole genome sequence data. Previous studies have evaluated models such as Enformer, but newer sequence-to-function models, including Borzoi and AlphaGenome, remain less well characterized for individual-level gene expression prediction, particularly in non-European and admixed populations. Here, we evaluated and fine-tuned Borzoi and AlphaGenome using personal genomes paired with whole-blood RNA-seq data from the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL). Fine-tuning substantially improved the performance of both sequence-based models compared with their pretrained versions; however, their performances remained similar to that of the variant-based linear models. Leveraging the ancestral diversity of HCHS/SOL, we found that Borzoi and AlphaGenome showed similar performance across Amerindian-, European-, and African-enriched groups. Fine-tuned Borzoi, fine-tuned AlphaGenome and elastic net performed modestly better when trained and evaluated in the same ancestry-enriched group. Finally, we explored strategies to improve prediction performance and found that incorporating predicted epigenetic features improved prediction near the promoter region. Significant progress remains needed before the full potential of sequence-based models is attained. Incorporating more biology-guided training approaches could be helpful to achieving better performance.

papers.title: VesiScope: A stand-alone tool for the automatic detection, quantification and size analysis of GUVs from phase contrast microscopy images
papers.abstract: Giant Unilamellar Vesicles (GUVs) are cell-sized phospholipid compartments that serve as versatile platforms for studying membrane-associated processes and engineering synthetic cell-like systems with applications spanning biophysics, synthetic biology, and, more recently, microrobotics. Fluorescence labeling is commonly used to enhance microscopy image contrast and facilitate automated Giant Unilamellar Vesicles (GUVs) quantification. Nonetheless, fluorescent probes may introduce unaccounted variations compared to the intended pristine formulation. Alternatively, phase-contrast microscopy enables label-free GUVs observation, but the lack of reliable automated detection methods limits high throughput analyses. To address this gap, we developed a framework based on YOLOv11 model, a state-of-art lightweight convolutional neural network for object detection. Trained on 4666 manually annotated GUVs from 164 phase-contrast microscope images, the model enables robust detection under low contrast-to-noise ratio and heterogeneous illumination. The trained model is implemented in a stand-alone desktop application supporting multiple analysis in a single run, pixel-to-micrometer calibration, and automated size distribution analysis. Retraining scripts compatible with standard hardware are also provided to enhance adaptability. VesiScope achieves high detection accuracy and competitive cross-microscope generalization enabling fast and reliable analysis of unaltered GUVs, supporting experimental reproducibility. By enabling rapid, reproducible, and label-free characterization of GUV populations, VesiScope provides a versatile tool for applications ranging from membrane biophysics and synthetic cell engineering to emerging GUV-based microrobotics, without introducing potentially perturbing fluorescent labels.

papers.title: A deep-learning predictive model for Cas12a activity in wheat
papers.abstract: CRISPR technology has created targeted DNA mutations across the tree of life. Target sites are defined by RNA molecules that largely determine the efficiency of an experiment. Several predictive models are available to select the most efficient RNAs. Unfortunately, these models are not built with plant data and have limited predictive power in plant systems. To overcome this limitation, we established a high-throughput arrayed wheat protoplast transfection method and measured the editing efficiency of ~1,000 unique LbCas12a crRNAs at on- and off-target sites. We trained different models by testing 40 deep learning architectures and found that a convolutional neural network model called 2CaP-5 displayed the best performance. While 2CaP-5 had moderate to strong predictive power in protoplasts, it did not generalize to Agrobacterium-mediated transformation. Despite this limitation, we demonstrate that 2CaP-5 can be re-trained with as few as 500 crRNAs. The use of such a small training set is advantageous for low-throughput experimental systems such as typically found in transgenic plant systems. We also used ~2,000 off-targets in the wheat subgenomes to investigate Cas12a specificity. Our dataset confirms previous observations regarding off-targets, specifically that single mismatches reduce indel efficiency provided they are adjacent to the PAM and that off-target activity can be largely prevented by three mismatches. Altogether, our results show that the 2CaP-5 model has moderate to strong predictive power for Cas12a crRNAs in wheat protoplasts and will serve as a useful foundation for predictive tools in other plant species.

papers.title: Curated annotations locate biological concepts in protein language models from layers to neurons
papers.abstract: Interpretability methods describe what a network has learned, yet their claims are rarely tested against model-independent ground truth. We argue that proteins are an ideal modality for interpretability since curators annotate functional sites residue by residue. Across three ESMC protein language models (300M-6B parameters), we show that conclusions depend on where models are read, how concepts are decoded, which units are examined, and how they are scored. Concepts become linearly readable along depth long before erasure impairs masked-token prediction, and 20-fold scaling shifts concept depth more than peak score. Most of a nonlinear probe's lead over a linear one reflects fitting and readout shape rather than nonlinear encoding. Over whole proteins, saturated metrics render feed-forward neurons indistinguishable from random rotations. At annotated residues, dual-signed neuron poles identify 2.5-5.4 times as many concepts as rotations without training, though sparse autoencoders identify more. Without held-out validation, however, shuffled annotations label nearly every latent, and causal reliance emerges in neuron groups rather than single poles. Reading selected intra-block states exposes binding and active sites that stream probes read poorly and lifts a simple probe 5% above the best published MCC on a leakage-controlled interaction benchmark. We recommend reading a model directly against annotation, scoring units where they fire with a measure that is not saturated, and training a dictionary only where it adds coverage.

papers.title: Mapping whole-tissue spatial multi-omics at single-cell resolution with STEP
papers.abstract: Spatial omics technologies have revolutionized our ability to map transcriptomic, proteomic, or metabolomic profiles within tissue contexts. However, existing spatial multi-omics approaches emphasize clustering or domain identification from measured profiles, while a general framework for whole-slice mapping in measured and unmeasured areas at single-cell resolution across additional omics layers remains lacking. Here we introduce STEP, a computational framework that integrates probabilistic inference with deep learning for flexible integration of histology, spatially resolved transcriptomics (SRT), single-cell, and/or multi-omics data. We validated STEP's advantages across diverse applications. Furthermore, STEP enables tri-modal integration of Xenium, CITE-seq, and imaging mass cytometry to map transcriptome-wide gene expression and protein profiles from a small gene panel. Through quadra-modal integration of SRT, histology, single-nucleus RNA sequencing, and inCITE-seq, STEP reconstructs a 3D multi-omics brain cell atlas from six low-resolution SRT sections. Collectively, STEP provides a cost-effective tool for exploring spatial biology by integrating diverse, complementary modalities.

papers.title: Deep Learning of Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Ophthalmoscopy for Type 2 Diabetes Classification
papers.abstract: PurposeTo evaluate whether fluorescence lifetime imaging ophthalmoscopy (FLIO) combined with deep learning can detect metabolic signatures for classification of type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM). DesignCross-sectional analysis of participants included in the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with FLIO imaging. Subjects1,783 participants from the AI-READI dataset (version 3) with HbA1c measurements and FLIO imaging scans: 425 normoglycemic, 569 prediabetic, and 789 diabetic. MethodsGlycemic groups were defined from self-reported diagnosis, glucose-lowering medication, and HbA1c. Center-of-mass mean lifetime ({tau}CMM) maps, corrected for background and system timing offset, were generated from the raw time-resolved FLIO scans. Group differences in central-window {tau}CMM were tested by one-way ANOVA and by age-adjusted analysis of covariance. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs), ResNet-18, and XGBoost were trained on {tau}CMM maps for three-class (normal, prediabetic, diabetic) and two binary (normal vs. impaired; normal vs. diabetic) classification of T2DM and compared them with an age-only classifier and with models combining FLIO and age. Main Outcome MeasuresMacro-averaged area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), sensitivity, specificity, accuracy, F1 score, and positive predictive value (PPV). ResultsGroup-averaged {tau}CMM was longer in prediabetic and diabetic than in normoglycemic participants in both the SSC (p < 0.001) and the LSC (p < 0.001), but only the SSC difference remained significant after age adjustment (p = 0.017). For 3-class classification, the CNN using FLIO achieved the highest AUROC (0.60 {+/-} 0.04), compared with 0.51 {+/-} 0.03 for an age-only classifier. ResNet-18 and XGBoost showed similar performance. Binary classification of normal vs. diabetic participants yielded AUROC 0.67 {+/-} 0.04 (CNN), 0.64 {+/-} 0.04 (ResNet-18), and 0.62 {+/-} 0.04 (XGBoost). All three FLIO models exceeded the age-only classifier in all T2DM classification tasks, whereas adding age to the FLIO models did not improve model performance. ConclusionsFLIO-derived {tau}CMM maps capture retinal signals associated with diabetes status that exceed what age alone provides, but yield modest classification performance with current artificial intelligence models. These findings highlight both the potential and the challenges of using FLIO for early metabolic screening and monitoring, informing future development of clinically applicable imaging biomarkers.

papers.title: Adversarial Robustness of Capsule Networks for Medical Image Classification
papers.abstract: PurposeDeep learning models are increasingly being used in medical diagnostics, but their vulnerability to adversarial perturbations raises concerns about their reliability in clinical applications. Capsule networks (CapsNets) are a promising architecture for medical imaging tasks, given their ability to model spatial relationships and train with smaller amounts of data. Although previous studies have focused on adversarial training approaches to improve robustness, exploring alternative architectures is an underexplored direction for combating poor adversarial stability. Prior work has suggested that CapsNets may exhibit improved robustness to adversarial perturbations compared to convolutional neural networks (CNNs), but performance on adversarial images has not been studied systematically in clinical environments. We evaluated the robustness of CapsNets compared to CNNs and vision transformers (ViTs) across multiple medical image classification tasks. MethodsWe trained two CNNs (ResNet-18 and ResNet-50), one ViT (MedViT), and two CapsNets (DR-CapsNet and BP-CapsNet) on four distinct medical imaging datasets (PneumoniaMNIST, BreastMNIST, NoduleMNIST3D, and BloodMNIST) and one natural image dataset (MNIST). Models were evaluated on adversarial examples generated by projected gradient descent, fast gradient sign method, AutoAttack, Carlini & Wagner, and black-box transfer attacks. Models also underwent PGD adversarial fine-tuning to assess whether architectural differences persisted after adversarial training. Interpretability experiments, including latent space and Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) analyses, were conducted to better understand model stability on adversarial inputs. ResultsUnder conventional training, CapsNets demonstrated superior robustness under adversarial perturbations compared to CNNs and ViTs across all medical imaging datasets and the natural image dataset. Latent space and Grad-CAM visualizations revealed that CapsNets maintained more consistent feature representations and attention maps after adversarial perturbations compared to CNNs and ViTs, suggesting that advantages in CapsNet robustness are supported, at least in part, by more stable feature encodings. PGD adversarial fine-tuning improved robustness across models, with MedViT exhibiting the largest gains and thereby narrowing the performance gap. ConclusionCapsNets exhibit advantages in adversarial robustness over CNN- and ViT-based models on medical imaging tasks. These findings suggest that capsule-based architectures may be a promising direction for robust medical image classification. Future work should validate CapsNet robustness across more complex medical imaging tasks, independent external datasets, and broader sources of real-world imaging variability.

papers.title: Discovery and Cross-Omic Replication of a Candidate Plasma Proteomic Signature for Anti-TNF Response in Crohn's Disease
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: Despite expanding therapeutic options for Crohn's disease (CD), treatment selection remains largely empiric. Identifying biomarkers linking inflammatory endotypes to treatment outcomes could inform first-line therapy selection. We sought to identify baseline plasma proteins associated with clinical, biochemical, and endoscopic outcomes in patients with CD receiving anti-TNF therapy. Methods: In this prospective multicenter cohort, children and young adults with CD initiating infliximab or adalimumab underwent plasma proteomic profiling at baseline and months 3 and 12 using SomaScan v4.1 (7,322 analytes) with deep remission (clinical and endoscopic) as the primary outcome. Rank-based composite correlation analysis identified candidate proteins associated with prespecified treatment outcomes, followed by functional enrichment analyses. Regularized machine learning models were used to derive and evaluate a candidate protein signature. Results: In a cohort of 80 participants, mean age 13.7 (SD 3.5) years, 42.5% female, and 90% White, composite rank analysis identified 73 candidate proteins associated with one or more outcomes. Seven candidate proteins (IFNA6, IGHM, MBL2, UBASH3A, REG1A, GABBR2, and NTS) were retained for evaluation. In an independent adult cohort (n=324), models based on whole-blood expression of the seven corresponding genes achieved mean AUPRCs of 0.71 (baseline) and 0.76 (week 14) for the cohort-defined primary response outcome. Conclusions: Plasma proteomic profiling identified a candidate 7-protein signature associated with anti-TNF treatment outcomes in CD. Cross-omic replication demonstrated consistent outcome-associated signals in an independent cohort. Although orthogonal validation of the protein signature is needed, these findings support the potential of proteomic biomarkers to guide biologically informed treatment selection.

papers.title: ST-FateFlow: Continuous Gene-Spatial Reconstruction with Differentiation-Potential Learning from Time-Resolved Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Time-resolved spatial transcriptomics provides a powerful view of dynamic biological processes by measuring cellular states together with their spatial organization across time. However, destructive profiling and experimental cost restrict observations to a few discrete time points collected from independent samples, with no known cell pairing across time. This makes it difficult to reconstruct gene expression and tissue organization at unobserved stages and to characterize differentiation-associated dynamics. Here, we introduce ST-FateFlow, a flow-matching framework for continuous gene-spatial dynamics and differentiation-potential learning. ST-FateFlow jointly learns gene-expression and spatial-coordinate velocity fields, enabling interpolation of missing time points and continuous modeling of transcriptional evolution and tissue remodeling. In parallel, it independently learns a time-conditioned differentiation potential, whose values organize cell states along inferred differentiation progressions and support the analysis of differentiation-associated transcriptional changes. Across multiple time-resolved spatial transcriptomics datasets, ST-FateFlow effectively captures coordinated gene-expression and spatial dynamics. Case studies further show that the learned potential landscapes are consistent with known developmental and regenerative trajectories and help identify candidate genes associated with differentiation progression.

papers.title: Read Before You Fit: Text-Derived Constraints for Discovering Differential Equations from Noisy Biological Data
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used for scientific equation discovery. However, most existing methods are strongly data-driven and assume sufficiently clean and representative observations. This assumption is problematic in biological systems, where individual-level measurements are often sparse, noisy, heterogeneous, and expensive to obtain. While the underlying mechanisms are extensively described in scientific text, they are not explicitly used for the LLM based modeling of such systems. We introduce P2C, an agentic framework that translates textual descriptions of biological systems into a typed set of formal constraints, and use these constraints to restrict candidate ordinary differential equation (ODE) structures before numerical fitting. P2C consists of five stages: Text2Constraint extraction, ODE discovery, symbolic verification, parameter fitting, and model scoring. We evaluate P2C on four published ODE systems of acute inflammation and immune regulation, under clean and noisy observations. By progressively degrading the numerical evidence, we isolate when textual domain knowledge contributes beyond regression alone. Across the four systems, adding Text2Constraint reduces the worst form error from 1.397 to 0.499 on clean data and from 13.096 to 1.095 for data perturbed with Gaussian noise of $σ=0.1$; P2C also achieves lower form error and trajectory error than several LLM-based baselines over the tested noise range.

papers.title: Deep Learning–Based Multi-Omics Integration Robustly Predicts Survival in Liver Cancer
papers.abstract: Identifying robust survival subgroups of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) will significantly improve patient care. Currently, endeavor of integrating multi-omics data to explicitly predict HCC survival from multiple patient cohorts is lacking. To fill this gap, we present a deep learning (DL)–based model on HCC that robustly differentiates survival subpopulations of patients in six cohorts. We built the DL-based, survival-sensitive model on 360 HCC patients' data using RNA sequencing (RNA-Seq), miRNA sequencing (miRNA-Seq), and methylation data from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), which predicts prognosis as good as an alternative model where genomics and clinical data are both considered. This DL-based model provides two optimal subgroups of patients with significant survival differences (P = 7.13e−6) and good model fitness [concordance index (C-index) = 0.68]. More aggressive subtype is associated with frequent TP53 inactivation mutations, higher expression of stemness markers (KRT19 and EPCAM) and tumor marker BIRC5, and activated Wnt and Akt signaling pathways.
