We validated this multi-omics model on five external datasets of various omics types: LIRI-JP cohort (n = 230, C-index = 0.75), NCI cohort (n = 221, C-index = 0.67), Chinese cohort (n = 166, C-index = 0.69), E-TABM-36 cohort (n = 40, C-index = 0.77), and Hawaiian cohort (n = 27, C-index = 0.82). This is the first study to employ DL to identify multi-omics features linked to the differential survival of patients with HCC. Given its robustness over multiple cohorts, we expect this workflow to be useful at predicting HCC prognosis prediction. Clin Cancer Res; 24(6); 1248–59. ©2017 AACR.

papers.title: DeepImpute: an accurate, fast, and scalable deep neural network method to impute single-cell RNA-seq data
papers.abstract: Abstract Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) offers new opportunities to study gene expression of tens of thousands of single cells simultaneously. We present DeepImpute, a deep neural network-based imputation algorithm that uses dropout layers and loss functions to learn patterns in the data, allowing for accurate imputation. Overall, DeepImpute yields better accuracy than other six publicly available scRNA-seq imputation methods on experimental data, as measured by the mean squared error or Pearson’s correlation coefficient. DeepImpute is an accurate, fast, and scalable imputation tool that is suited to handle the ever-increasing volume of scRNA-seq data, and is freely available at https://github.com/lanagarmire/DeepImpute .

papers.title: Generating 3D molecules conditional on receptor binding sites with deep generative models
papers.abstract: The goal of structure-based drug discovery is to find small molecules that bind to a given target protein. Deep learning has been used to generate drug-like molecules with certain cheminformatic properties, but has not yet been applied to generating 3D molecules predicted to bind to proteins by sampling the conditional distribution of protein-ligand binding interactions. In this work, we describe for the first time a deep learning system for generating 3D molecular structures conditioned on a receptor binding site. We approach the problem using a conditional variational autoencoder trained on an atomic density grid representation of cross-docked protein-ligand structures. We apply atom fitting and bond inference procedures to construct valid molecular conformations from generated atomic densities. We evaluate the properties of the generated molecules and demonstrate that they change significantly when conditioned on mutated receptors. We also explore the latent space learned by our generative model using sampling and interpolation techniques. This work opens the door for end-to-end prediction of stable bioactive molecules from protein structures with deep learning.

papers.title: Solo: Doublet Identification in Single-Cell RNA-Seq via Semi-Supervised Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) measurements of gene expression enable an unprecedented high-resolution view into cellular state. However, current methods often result in two or more cells that share the same cell-identifying barcode; these "doublets" violate the fundamental premise of single-cell technology and can lead to incorrect inferences. Here, we describe Solo, a semi-supervised deep learning approach that identifies doublets with greater accuracy than existing methods. Solo embeds cells unsupervised using a variational autoencoder and then appends a feed-forward neural network layer to the encoder to form a supervised classifier. We train this classifier to distinguish simulated doublets from the observed data. Solo can be applied in combination with experimental doublet detection methods to further purify scRNA-seq data to true single cells. It is freely available from https://github.com/calico/solo. A record of this paper's transparent peer review process is included in the Supplemental Information.

papers.title: Realistic in silico generation and augmentation of single-cell RNA-seq data using generative adversarial networks
papers.abstract: A fundamental problem in biomedical research is the low number of observations available, mostly due to a lack of available biosamples, prohibitive costs, or ethical reasons. Augmenting few real observations with generated in silico samples could lead to more robust analysis results and a higher reproducibility rate. Here, we propose the use of conditional single-cell generative adversarial neural networks (cscGAN) for the realistic generation of single-cell RNA-seq data. cscGAN learns non-linear gene-gene dependencies from complex, multiple cell type samples and uses this information to generate realistic cells of defined types. Augmenting sparse cell populations with cscGAN generated cells improves downstream analyses such as the detection of marker genes, the robustness and reliability of classifiers, the assessment of novel analysis algorithms, and might reduce the number of animal experiments and costs in consequence. cscGAN outperforms existing methods for single-cell RNA-seq data generation in quality and hold great promise for the realistic generation and augmentation of other biomedical data types.

papers.title: SpaCell: integrating tissue morphology and spatial gene expression to predict disease cells
papers.abstract: MOTIVATION: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technology is increasingly being applied because it enables the measurement of spatial gene expression in an intact tissue along with imaging morphology of the same tissue. However, current analysis methods for ST data do not use image pixel information, thus missing the quantitative links between gene expression and tissue morphology. RESULTS: We developed a user-friendly deep learning software, SpaCell, to integrate millions of pixel intensity values with thousands of gene expression measurements from spatially barcoded spots in a tissue. We show the integration approach outperforms the use of gene-count data alone or imaging data alone to build deep learning models to identify cell types or predict labels of tissue images with high resolution and accuracy. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The SpaCell package is open source under an MIT licence and it is available at https://github.com/BiomedicalMachineLearning/SpaCell. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: ACTINN: automated identification of cell types in single cell RNA sequencing
papers.abstract: Abstract Motivation Cell type identification is one of the major goals in single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). Current methods for assigning cell types typically involve the use of unsupervised clustering, the identification of signature genes in each cluster, followed by a manual lookup of these genes in the literature and databases to assign cell types. However, there are several limitations associated with these approaches, such as unwanted sources of variation that influence clustering and a lack of canonical markers for certain cell types. Here, we present ACTINN (Automated Cell Type Identification using Neural Networks), which employs a neural network with three hidden layers, trains on datasets with predefined cell types and predicts cell types for other datasets based on the trained parameters. Results We trained the neural network on a mouse cell type atlas (Tabula Muris Atlas) and a human immune cell dataset, and used it to predict cell types for mouse leukocytes, human PBMCs and human T cell sub types. The results showed that our neural network is fast and accurate, and should therefore be a useful tool to complement existing scRNA-seq pipelines. Availability and implementation The codes and datasets are available at https://figshare.com/articles/ACTINN/8967116. Tutorial is available at https://github.com/mafeiyang/ACTINN. All codes are implemented in python. Supplementary information Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: MELD: Mutation Effect Learning through Differential embeddings
papers.abstract: We introduce MELD (Mutation Effect Learning through Differential Embeddings), a compact model for predicting the functional consequences of single nucleotide variants (SNVs) by training directly on the wild-type (WT) versus mutant differential. Interpreting SNVs is central to clinical genomics, yet experimental characterization cannot scale to millions of observed variants. Leading sequence-to-function models (Enformer, Borzoi, AlphaGenome) are trained on absolute genomic tracks and score variants post hoc through in-silico mutagenesis (ISM), so the WT-mutant difference never enters the training loss. MELD instead places the logit difference {Delta}z = zmut - zwt inside the supervised objective. It combines a shared CNN-Transformer encoder, a mutant-specific mutation-mask boost, multiscale mutation-centered pooling, and a learned adaptive amplification factor . On ClinVar (1.57M variants), MELD (1.9M parameters) reached an AUROC of 0.986 versus 0.800 for a same-data, same-backbone ISM baseline, with ablations confirming the contribution of each component. On a shared benchmark, it outperformed frozen foundation models with 3-1,300x more parameters (AUROC 0.967 vs. 0.924 for AlphaGenome and 0.936 for Nucleotide Transformer). With only 50, 000 training variants, it exceeded the ISM baseline trained on all 1.48M (AUROC 0.903 vs. 0.796) variants. On BRCA1 saturation genome editing, frozen MELD achieved a Spearman {rho} of 0.42, above Borzoi (0.40), and ClinVar transfer raised it to 0.45. These results demonstrate that direct differential supervision is a compact, data-efficient alternative to post-hoc ISM scoring with substantially larger pretrained models.

papers.title: Transformer for one stop interpretable cell type annotation
papers.abstract: Consistent annotation transfer from reference dataset to query dataset is fundamental to the development and reproducibility of single-cell research. Compared with traditional annotation methods, deep learning based methods are faster and more automated. A series of useful single cell analysis tools based on autoencoder architecture have been developed but these struggle to strike a balance between depth and interpretability. Here, we present TOSICA, a multi-head self-attention deep learning model based on Transformer that enables interpretable cell type annotation using biologically understandable entities, such as pathways or regulons. We show that TOSICA achieves fast and accurate one-stop annotation and batch-insensitive integration while providing biologically interpretable insights for understanding cellular behavior during development and disease progressions. We demonstrate TOSICA's advantages by applying it to scRNA-seq data of tumor-infiltrating immune cells, and CD14+ monocytes in COVID-19 to reveal rare cell types, heterogeneity and dynamic trajectories associated with disease progression and severity.

papers.title: DynamicBind: predicting ligand-specific protein-ligand complex structure with a deep equivariant generative model
papers.abstract: While significant advances have been made in predicting static protein structures, the inherent dynamics of proteins, modulated by ligands, are crucial for understanding protein function and facilitating drug discovery. Traditional docking methods, frequently used in studying protein-ligand interactions, typically treat proteins as rigid. While molecular dynamics simulations can propose appropriate protein conformations, they're computationally demanding due to rare transitions between biologically relevant equilibrium states. In this study, we present DynamicBind, a deep learning method that employs equivariant geometric diffusion networks to construct a smooth energy landscape, promoting efficient transitions between different equilibrium states. DynamicBind accurately recovers ligand-specific conformations from unbound protein structures without the need for holo-structures or extensive sampling. Remarkably, it demonstrates state-of-the-art performance in docking and virtual screening benchmarks. Our experiments reveal that DynamicBind can accommodate a wide range of large protein conformational changes and identify cryptic pockets in unseen protein targets. As a result, DynamicBind shows potential in accelerating the development of small molecules for previously undruggable targets and expanding the horizons of computational drug discovery.

papers.title: Folding non-homologous proteins by coupling deep-learning contact maps with I-TASSER assembly simulations
papers.abstract: Structure prediction for proteins lacking homologous templates in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) remains a significant unsolved problem. We developed a protocol, C-I-TASSER, to integrate interresidue contact maps from deep neural-network learning with the cutting-edge I-TASSER fragment assembly simulations. Large-scale benchmark tests showed that C-I-TASSER can fold more than twice the number of non-homologous proteins than the I-TASSER, which does not use contacts. When applied to a folding experiment on 8,266 unsolved Pfam families, C-I-TASSER successfully folded 4,162 domain families, including 504 folds that are not found in the PDB. Furthermore, it created correct folds for 85% of proteins in the SARS-CoV-2 genome, despite the quick mutation rate of the virus and sparse sequence profiles. The results demonstrated the critical importance of coupling whole-genome and metagenome-based evolutionary information with optimal structure assembly simulations for solving the problem of non-homologous protein structure prediction.

papers.title: Artificial Intelligence in Oncology: Current Capabilities, Future Opportunities, and Ethical Considerations
papers.abstract: The promise of highly personalized oncology care using artificial intelligence (AI) technologies has been forecasted since the emergence of the field. Cumulative advances across the science are bringing this promise to realization, including refinement of machine learning- and deep learning algorithms; expansion in the depth and variety of databases, including multiomics; and the decreased cost of massively parallelized computational power. Examples of successful clinical applications of AI can be found throughout the cancer continuum and in multidisciplinary practice, with computer vision-assisted image analysis in particular having several U.S. Food and Drug Administration-approved uses. Techniques with emerging clinical utility include whole blood multicancer detection from deep sequencing, virtual biopsies, natural language processing to infer health trajectories from medical notes, and advanced clinical decision support systems that combine genomics and clinomics. Substantial issues have delayed broad adoption, with data transparency and interpretability suffering from AI's "black box" mechanism, and intrinsic bias against underrepresented persons limiting the reproducibility of AI models and perpetuating health care disparities. Midfuture projections of AI maturation involve increasing a model's complexity by using multimodal data elements to better approximate an organic system. Far-future positing includes living databases that accumulate all aspects of a person's health into discrete data elements; this will fuel highly convoluted modeling that can tailor treatment selection, dose determination, surveillance modality and schedule, and more. The field of AI has had a historical dichotomy between its proponents and detractors. The successful development of recent applications, and continued investment in prospective validation that defines their impact on multilevel outcomes, has established a momentum of accelerated progress.
papers.venue: American Society of Clinical Oncology Educational Book

papers.title: Practical evaluation of AI models to forecast a respiratory seasonal epidemic in Canada
papers.abstract: Public health organizations can benefit greatly from infectious disease epidemic forecasting to guide and support interventions and policies that reduce morbidity. However, accurate and reliable epidemic forecasting remains notoriously challenging and is an evolving field in which new scientific advances continue to support forecasting efforts. Computational models that underpin artificial intelligence (AI) models are promising developments that may improve seasonal epidemic forecasting. This study aims to compare the performance of a selection of AI models previously identified as well adapted to epidemic forecasting, including machine learning (XGBoost), deep learning models (Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU), Transformer), time-series foundation model (Chronos), and a hybrid model: physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), against statistical models (Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA), Prophet) and a compartmental epidemiological model (CEM) in seasonal epidemic forecasting across Canada. The study uses weekly positivity-rate incidence of seasonal influenza A across eight Canadian provinces during the 2025/2026 season as a test case. Each model generated short-term (up to 5 weeks ahead) forecasts independently for each province from October 11, 2025, to March 28, 2026. We evaluated performance using mean absolute error (MAE) for each province. Our results show that AI models, specifically GRU, Transformer, and Chronos models, achieve lower MAE than CEM in four of eight provinces (Alberta, British Columbia, Prince Edward Island, and Saskatchewan). Meanwhile, CEM and ARIMA outperform all AI models in three provinces (Ontario, Quebec, Manitoba) and one province (Nova Scotia), respectively. Furthermore, data pooling strategies that leverage multi-province data for the target virus or multi-virus data within individual provinces greatly improve deep learning models, and Chronos performs well under zero-shot forecasting in British Columbia. In contrast, Prophet always has the highest MAE, and PINN is worse than CEMs. Overall, AI models performed comparably to, or slightly better than, CEMs. However, these modest gains may not offset their lack of interpretability, high computational costs, and reliance on the specialized expertise required for implementation. We therefore conclude that AI models are best as a complement, rather than a replacement, to CEMs, which remain crucial for interpretability and informing decision-making.

papers.title: Clustering of single-cell multi-omics data with a multimodal deep learning method
papers.abstract: Single-cell multimodal sequencing technologies are developed to simultaneously profile different modalities of data in the same cell. It provides a unique opportunity to jointly analyze multimodal data at the single-cell level for the identification of distinct cell types. A correct clustering result is essential for the downstream complex biological functional studies. However, combining different data sources for clustering analysis of single-cell multimodal data remains a statistical and computational challenge. Here, we develop a novel multimodal deep learning method, scMDC, for single-cell multi-omics data clustering analysis. scMDC is an end-to-end deep model that explicitly characterizes different data sources and jointly learns latent features of deep embedding for clustering analysis. Extensive simulation and real-data experiments reveal that scMDC outperforms existing single-cell single-modal and multimodal clustering methods on different single-cell multimodal datasets. The linear scalability of running time makes scMDC a promising method for analyzing large multimodal datasets.

papers.title: DeepST: identifying spatial domains in spatial transcriptomics by deep learning
papers.abstract: Recent advances in spatial transcriptomics (ST) have brought unprecedented opportunities to understand tissue organization and function in spatial context. However, it is still challenging to precisely dissect spatial domains with similar gene expression and histology in situ. Here, we present DeepST, an accurate and universal deep learning framework to identify spatial domains, which performs better than the existing state-of-the-art methods on benchmarking datasets of the human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. Further testing on a breast cancer ST dataset, we showed that DeepST can dissect spatial domains in cancer tissue at a finer scale. Moreover, DeepST can achieve not only effective batch integration of ST data generated from multiple batches or different technologies, but also expandable capabilities for processing other spatial omics data. Together, our results demonstrate that DeepST has the exceptional capacity for identifying spatial domains, making it a desirable tool to gain novel insights from ST studies.

papers.title: Efficient prediction of a spatial transcriptomics profile better characterizes breast cancer tissue sections without costly experimentation
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics is an emerging technology requiring costly reagents and considerable skills, limiting the identification of transcriptional markers related to histology. Here, we show that predicted spatial gene-expression in unmeasured regions and tissues can enhance biologists' histological interpretations. We developed the Deep learning model for Spatial gene Clusters and Expression, DeepSpaCE, and confirmed its performance using the spatial-transcriptome profiles and immunohistochemistry images of consecutive human breast cancer tissue sections. For example, the predicted expression patterns of SPARC, an invasion marker, highlighted a small tumor-invasion region difficult to identify using raw spatial transcriptome data alone because of a lack of measurements. We further developed semi-supervised DeepSpaCE using unlabeled histology images and increased the imputation accuracy of consecutive sections, enhancing applicability for a small sample size. Our method enables users to derive hidden histological characters via spatial transcriptome and gene annotations, leading to accelerated biological discoveries without additional experiments.

papers.title: Generative modeling of single-cell time series with PRESCIENT enables prediction of cell trajectories with interventions
papers.abstract: Abstract Existing computational methods that use single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) for cell fate prediction do not model how cells evolve stochastically and in physical time, nor can they predict how differentiation trajectories are altered by proposed interventions. We introduce PRESCIENT (Potential eneRgy undErlying Single Cell gradIENTs), a generative modeling framework that learns an underlying differentiation landscape from time-series scRNA-seq data. We validate PRESCIENT on an experimental lineage tracing dataset, where we show that PRESCIENT is able to predict the fate biases of progenitor cells in hematopoiesis when accounting for cell proliferation, improving upon the best-performing existing method. We demonstrate how PRESCIENT can simulate trajectories for perturbed cells, recovering the expected effects of known modulators of cell fate in hematopoiesis and pancreatic β cell differentiation. PRESCIENT is able to accommodate complex perturbations of multiple genes, at different time points and from different starting cell populations, and is available at https://github.com/gifford-lab/prescient .

papers.title: DeepTCR is a deep learning framework for revealing sequence concepts within T-cell repertoires
papers.abstract: Deep learning algorithms have been utilized to achieve enhanced performance in pattern-recognition tasks. The ability to learn complex patterns in data has tremendous implications in immunogenomics. T-cell receptor (TCR) sequencing assesses the diversity of the adaptive immune system and allows for modeling its sequence determinants of antigenicity. We present DeepTCR, a suite of unsupervised and supervised deep learning methods able to model highly complex TCR sequencing data by learning a joint representation of a TCR by its CDR3 sequences and V/D/J gene usage. We demonstrate the utility of deep learning to provide an improved 'featurization' of the TCR across multiple human and murine datasets, including improved classification of antigen-specific TCRs and extraction of antigen-specific TCRs from noisy single-cell RNA-Seq and T-cell culture-based assays. Our results highlight the flexibility and capacity for deep neural networks to extract meaningful information from complex immunogenomic data for both descriptive and predictive purposes.

papers.title: DNABERT-S: pioneering species differentiation with species-aware DNA embeddings
papers.abstract: SUMMARY: We introduce DNABERT-S, a tailored genome model that develops species-aware embeddings to naturally cluster and segregate DNA sequences of different species in the embedding space. Differentiating species from genomic sequences (i.e. DNA and RNA) is vital yet challenging, since many real-world species remain uncharacterized, lacking known genomes for reference. Embedding-based methods are therefore used to differentiate species in an unsupervised manner. DNABERT-S builds upon a pre-trained genome foundation model named DNABERT-2. To encourage effective embeddings to error-prone long-read DNA sequences, we introduce Manifold Instance Mixup (MI-Mix), a contrastive objective that mixes the hidden representations of DNA sequences at randomly selected layers and trains the model to recognize and differentiate these mixed proportions at the output layer. We further enhance it with the proposed Curriculum Contrastive Learning (C2LR) strategy. Empirical results on 28 diverse datasets show DNABERT-S's effectiveness, especially in realistic label-scarce scenarios. For example, it identifies twice more species from a mixture of unlabeled genomic sequences, doubles the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) in species clustering, and outperforms the top baseline's performance in 10-shot species classification with just a 2-shot training. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Model, codes, and data are publically available at https://github.com/MAGICS-LAB/DNABERT_S.

papers.title: De novo design of protein structure and function with RFdiffusion
papers.abstract: There has been considerable recent progress in designing new proteins using deep-learning methods 1–9 . Despite this progress, a general deep-learning framework for protein design that enables solution of a wide range of design challenges, including de novo binder design and design of higher-order symmetric architectures, has yet to be described. Diffusion models 10,11 have had considerable success in image and language generative modelling but limited success when applied to protein modelling, probably due to the complexity of protein backbone geometry and sequence–structure relationships. Here we show that by fine-tuning the RoseTTAFold structure prediction network on protein structure denoising tasks, we obtain a generative model of protein backbones that achieves outstanding performance on unconditional and topology-constrained protein monomer design, protein binder design, symmetric oligomer design, enzyme active site scaffolding and symmetric motif scaffolding for therapeutic and metal-binding protein design. We demonstrate the power and generality of the method, called RoseTTAFold diffusion (RFdiffusion), by experimentally characterizing the structures and functions of hundreds of designed symmetric assemblies, metal-binding proteins and protein binders. The accuracy of RFdiffusion is confirmed by the cryogenic electron microscopy structure of a designed binder in complex with influenza haemagglutinin that is nearly identical to the design model. In a manner analogous to networks that produce images from user-specified inputs, RFdiffusion enables the design of diverse functional proteins from simple molecular specifications.

papers.title: Robust deep learning–based protein sequence design using ProteinMPNN
papers.abstract: Although deep learning has revolutionized protein structure prediction, almost all experimentally characterized de novo protein designs have been generated using physically based approaches such as Rosetta. Here, we describe a deep learning–based protein sequence design method, ProteinMPNN, that has outstanding performance in both in silico and experimental tests. On native protein backbones, ProteinMPNN has a sequence recovery of 52.4% compared with 32.9% for Rosetta. The amino acid sequence at different positions can be coupled between single or multiple chains, enabling application to a wide range of current protein design challenges. We demonstrate the broad utility and high accuracy of ProteinMPNN using x-ray crystallography, cryo–electron microscopy, and functional studies by rescuing previously failed designs, which were made using Rosetta or AlphaFold, of protein monomers, cyclic homo-oligomers, tetrahedral nanoparticles, and target-binding proteins.

papers.title: DNABERT: pre-trained Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers model for DNA-language in genome
papers.abstract: MOTIVATION: Deciphering the language of non-coding DNA is one of the fundamental problems in genome research. Gene regulatory code is highly complex due to the existence of polysemy and distant semantic relationship, which previous informatics methods often fail to capture especially in data-scarce scenarios. RESULTS: To address this challenge, we developed a novel pre-trained bidirectional encoder representation, named DNABERT, to capture global and transferrable understanding of genomic DNA sequences based on up and downstream nucleotide contexts. We compared DNABERT to the most widely used programs for genome-wide regulatory elements prediction and demonstrate its ease of use, accuracy and efficiency. We show that the single pre-trained transformers model can simultaneously achieve state-of-the-art performance on prediction of promoters, splice sites and transcription factor binding sites, after easy fine-tuning using small task-specific labeled data. Further, DNABERT enables direct visualization of nucleotide-level importance and semantic relationship within input sequences for better interpretability and accurate identification of conserved sequence motifs and functional genetic variant candidates. Finally, we demonstrate that pre-trained DNABERT with human genome can even be readily applied to other organisms with exceptional performance. We anticipate that the pre-trained DNABERT model can be fined tuned to many other sequence analyses tasks. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The source code, pretrained and finetuned model for DNABERT are available at GitHub (https://github.com/jerryji1993/DNABERT). SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

papers.title: Hypothalamic volume and cell-type changes in ageing and Alzheimer's disease.
papers.abstract: Alterations in metabolism, stress response, sleep, circadian rhythms and neuroendocrine processes are key features of ageing and neurodegeneration1,2. These fundamental processes are regulated by the hypothalamus, yet how its functionally distinct subregions and cell types change during human ageing and Alzheimer's disease (AD) remains largely unexplored. Here we present HypoAD, an atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, including high-resolution magnetic resonance imaging from 458 individuals and single-nucleus RNA sequencing of 614,403 nuclei from young participants, patients with AD and age-matched non-dementia control participants. We show that hypothalamic subregions governing metabolism, stress and circadian rhythms are particularly vulnerable, showing notable changes in both volumes and gene expression during ageing and AD. At the molecular level, machine learning models identified the inflammatory response and regulators of circadian rhythms as key cellular predictors of AD. These signatures were reflected in specific cell types: microglia transitioned to a pro-inflammatory state, whereas inhibitory neurons within sleep-regulating and circadian-regulating hypothalamic subregions showed the most profound transcriptional alterations, including disruptions in ligand-receptor interactions and G-protein-coupled receptor signalling. HypoAD provides a high-resolution volumetric map and a transcriptomic atlas of the human hypothalamus in ageing and AD, relating lifestyle and behavioural changes to the relevant volumetric and molecular pathways. In addition, HypoAD provides a framework to investigate hypothalamic dysfunction and establishes a roadmap for targeted interventions aimed at mitigating physiological disruptions to potentially slow disease progression.

papers.title: De novo design of lipopeptides with antimicrobial potency enabled by a chain-as-prompt deep learning framework.
papers.abstract: Antimicrobial lipopeptides (AMLPs) represent a promising solution to global antibiotic crisis, yet their precision design remains challenging due to the inability of current computational models to account for N-terminal fatty acid modification. Here we develop a deep learning-driven AMLP model for de novo design of AMLPs by integrating a chain-as-prompt mechanism with domain-adaptive transfer learning, effectively bridging the representation gap between peptide sequence and lipid-induced bioactivity. Using the AMLP model, 2657 evolutionarily selected RiPP-derived core peptide sequences from 96,911 bacterial genomes are inspiringly designed for virtual lipidation with seven N-terminal fatty acid chains (C6-C18) followed by predictive screening, generating 6197 candidate sequences. Notably, we find that both high KRH rate ( ≥ 0.3) and common fatty acid tails (C12 and C16) are also critical for further selection of candidate AMLPs, resulting in 289 sequences. Then, 46 are randomly synthesized, with 44 showing antimicrobial activities (a positive rate of 95.7%). The lead antibiotic LP630 exhibits broad-spectrum activities against typical Gram-positive, Gram-negative and mycobacterial strains by targeting multiple bacterial cell membrane components, and demonstrates potent therapeutic efficacy in murine wound infection models. Our study provides a streamlined and universal paradigm for deep learning-enabled high-throughput discovery of novel lipopeptide therapeutics.

papers.title: Bacterial protein function prediction via multimodal deep learning.
papers.abstract: Bacterial proteins are specialized with extensive functional diversity for survival in diverse and stressful environments. A significant portion of these proteins remains functionally uncharacterized, limiting our understanding of bacterial survival mechanisms. Hence, we develop Deep Expression STructure (DeepEST), a multimodal deep learning framework that predicts protein function in bacteria by assigning Gene Ontology (GO) terms. DeepEST comprises two modules: a multi-layer perceptron that uses gene expression and gene location, and a protein structure-based module that uses predicted structures and amino acid sequences. Within DeepEST, we integrate these modules through a learnable weighted linear combination and introduce a novel masked loss function to fine-tune the structure-based predictor for bacterial species. These choices are well suited for bacteria, in which functionally related genes frequently colocalize and are cotranscribed within operons, allowing transcription dynamics to serve as informative, condition-dependent signals. We show that DeepEST outperforms existing protein function prediction methods on a 25-species benchmark, relying solely on amino acid sequence or protein structure. Averaged over the 25 species, DeepEST reaches a protein-centric F max of 0.689 and a term-centric micro-AUPRC of 0.756, a relative improvement of 4.4% and 11.6% over the second-best method, the structure-based predictor DeepFRI. Moreover, DeepEST predicts GO terms for unclassified hypothetical proteins across 25 human bacterial pathogens, supporting their experimental characterization. DeepEST bridges organism-specific data integration and structure-based transfer learning, providing a method tailored for bacterial protein function prediction in settings with structural and multi-condition expression data.

papers.title: Explainable AI identifies recombination and chromatin environment as key predictors of subgenome evolution in maize and Brassica.
papers.abstract: Polyploidy, or whole genome duplication, reshapes genomes through biased gene loss and regulatory rewiring, yet the drivers of biased fractionation among subgenomes remain unclear. Using maize and Brassica rapa as model allopolyploids, we compiled 60 genomic and epigenomic features in maize and 45 in B. rapa and constructed supervised machine learning models to classify genes by subgenome identity. In both species, eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) approaches identified recombination rate as the most influential and highly interconnected feature despite nonsignificant mean differences between subgenome groups. Chromosome location, transposon density, and chromatin-associated features, including the proximity of accessible chromatin regions to genes and active histone marks such as H3K9ac and H3K27ac, consistently ranked among the top contributors to subgenome classification. XAI-derived covariation and interaction networks further revealed recombination rate as the central node connecting significant features. Together, these results highlight recombination and chromatin environment as major predictors of subgenome divergence in polyploid genomes.

papers.title: R-loopBase v2.0: species- and cell type-resolved quantitative R-loop maps and R-loop regulatory resources.
papers.abstract: R-loops are non-canonical nucleic acid structures implicated in diverse cellular processes and diseases. We previously developed R-loopBase to address the pressing challenges of inaccurate R-loop maps and the limited understanding of the R-loop regulatory network. However, R-loopBase provided only human R-loop maps with categorical confidence and did not account for cell type specificity. These limitations, coupled with the emerging R-loop profiling technologies and advances in R-loop regulatory mechanisms, have motivated the development of R-loopBase v2.0 (https://rloopbase.nju.edu.cn). After uniformly re-analysing 358 R-loop mapping datasets generated by 16 technologies, we introduce a quantitative R-loop scoring framework that assesses genome-wide R-loop confidence in human, demonstrating strong concordance with known R-loop biology. We further extend the framework to specific cell types and mouse, fruit fly, and yeast. In parallel, we substantially expand the collection of R-loop regulators across species, enabling the inference of changes in R-loop homeostasis. Building on these expanded datasets, we implement several new interactive features and analytical tools, including an expanded multi-species genome browser, deep learning-based R-loop prediction, R-loop homeostasis analysis, and a streamlined data download portal. We anticipate that R-loopBase v2.0 will serve as an enhanced, up-to-date one-stop resource for the R-loop research community.

papers.title: A framework for genome-wide characterization of DNA methylation and variant effect prediction.
papers.abstract: DNA methylation plays a critical role in many essential biological processes, including transcriptional regulation, genomic imprinting, chromosomal maintenance, genomic stability and development, and has phenotypic and disease impacts. However, genome-wide characterization of methylation patterns across cell types and tissues remains a major challenge. Here, to address this, we present a framework that enables systematic genome-wide analysis of methylation and sequence-based prediction of context-specific methylation effects of variants. Our data-driven discovery of methylation classes reveals context-dependent roles for methylation across tissues, cell types and regions of the genome. The framework also includes Wreath, a deep learning-based sequence model specifically designed to accurately predict the context-dependent impact of any genetic variant on methylation. These developments leverage a compendium that harmonizes disparate methylation profiles from disparate studies including over 90 tissues and cell types. Using Wreath, we systematically characterized the impact of noncoding pathogenic variants on tissue-specific methylation, generating mechanistic hypotheses for individual regulatory variants. We make the full framework, including the compendium, the methylation classes and the model, available for use by the community.

papers.title: Reconstructing the single-cell spatiotemporal dynamics of glioblastoma invasion.
papers.abstract: Glioblastoma invasion into healthy brain tissue remains a major barrier to effective treatment, but the dynamic single-cell behaviors underlying this process remain difficult to measure across patient models. Here, we introduce GlioTrace, an ex vivo imaging and computational framework for real-time tracking of glioblastoma invasion in patient-derived xenograft brain slices. Combining whole-specimen confocal microscopy with machine learning-based morphology classification and probabilistic modeling of state transitions, GlioTrace reconstructs how tumor cells switch between invasion phenotypes and how these dynamics are shaped by local tissue context and therapy. Across six patient-derived models, GlioTrace reveals that invasion plasticity is patient-specific, spatially organized, and modulated by vascular proximity and microglial interaction. Targeted therapies selectively alter phenotype composition and transition probabilities, whereas standard-of-care treatment enriches a highly motile, transition-connected branching state consistent with a treatment-tolerant invasive phenotype. Thus, GlioTrace makes glioblastoma invasion a measurable dynamic process for comparing patient-specific treatment responses in living brain tissue.

papers.title: Toward planetary microbial systems biology.
papers.abstract: Microorganisms underpin Earth's biosphere, sustaining life, shaping biogeochemical cycles, and maintaining ecosystem stability. In an era of scientific and geopolitical fragmentation, we advocate for a "planetary microbial systems biology" (PMSB) framework to uncover the mechanisms and organizational principles governing Earth's interconnected microbial systems across scales of matter, space, and time and in relation to underlying natural and anthropogenic drivers. PMSB combines molecular and cellular technologies, multi-omics data, artificial intelligence (AI), and integrated transdisciplinary research across ecosystems. By federating open data and combining field observations, experimentation, and modeling, PMSB enables predictive understanding of microbiome dynamics across planetary scales, thus filling a critical knowledge gap in our understanding of the co-evolution of life and the Earth-system.

papers.title: HRDPath: an explainable multi-model deep learning architecture for predicting homologous recombination deficiency from histopathology images.
papers.abstract: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) is a critical biomarker for guiding treatment decisions in high-grade serous tubo-ovarian carcinoma (HGSOC), a cancer with few reliable biomarkers. However, existing genomics-based tests for HRD are variable, expensive, and time-consuming. We develop HRDPath, a patient-level deep learning architecture that predicts HRD status from whole slide images, requiring no additional molecular testing. HRDPath is validated across three cohorts of female patients and achieves an AUC of 0.846, significantly outperforming previously reported results in HGSOC. By incorporating multiple slides per patient and targeted optimization strategies, we strengthen the model clinical utility, with both specificity and sensitivity reaching 0.90. Our interpretability pipeline enhances model trustworthiness and reveals important clinical and biological insights into HRD-positive cancers, highlighting the associated morphological and pathological changes at the cellular and tissue levels. HRDPath provides a foundation for an accessible and scalable digital biomarker to improve treatment stratification in ovarian cancer globally.

papers.title: Short-term memory of past caspase activity biases cell elimination in vivo.
papers.abstract: Apoptosis is triggered by the activation of Caspases leading to irreversible engagement in cell death. However, recent data outline numerous non-apoptotic functions of caspases as well as quite ubiquitous sublethal activation of effector caspases in vivo, opening the question of what drives the bifurcation between cell death and survival. Using quantitative live imaging combined with machine learning and optogenetics in the Drosophila pupal notum (a single-layer epithelium), we reveal the existence of a large heterogeneity of caspase activity thresholds between cells and distinct spatial domains with low or high sensitivity to caspases. We outline the central role of past exposure to sublethal caspase activity, which sensitises cells to apoptosis for several hours and reduces their threshold, and can bias single-cell elimination. Altogether, this work reveals the role of a cell's past history for apoptosis regulation in vivo, which can bias clonal selection and the spatial pattern of cell death.

papers.title: Is the Bitter Lesson coming to genomic prediction? An untuned tabular foundation model matches or beats specialized methods
papers.abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) is dominated by models designed around assumptions about how genetic variation affects phenotypes. Here we asked how well a general-purpose pretrained tabular foundation model called TabPFN-3.5 does with no genetics-specific modeling and no tuning when given marker genotypes directly. We benchmarked TabPFN-3.5 using a published comparison of 18 GP methods on 18 traits in six plant species. Against the published means, TabPFN-3.5 ranked first on 11 of 18 traits and had the best median rank. Because the published benchmark did not identify its test sets, we reran GBLUP, RKHS and elastic-net models on the same splits as TabPFN-3.5. Against the best of these, TabPFN-3.5 was significantly behind on only one trait, spruce wood density, and ahead on 12 of 18, with significant gains on all three soybean traits and rice flowering time. In the soybean panel, which had the largest number of lines, its advantage was clearest. In leave-families-out cross-validation, where models were trained on some soybean families and used to predict lines from other families withheld from training, every model lost accuracy and TabPFN-3.5 performed on par with GBLUP and RKHS. That a general-purpose learner matches or exceeds decades of specialized GP models is consistent with Sutton's Bitter Lesson, which holds that methods that scale with computation eventually overtake those built on human knowledge of the domain.

papers.title: Biomolecular design through latent reasoning with RFD4-Proteina
papers.abstract: Biomolecular design requires finding chemically and geometrically compatible arrangements of interacting atoms and molecules. The complexity of problems which can be tackled by deep learning design models is limited by both the molecular landscape they encompass and their ability to explore that landscape effectively. Here we introduce RFD4-Proteina, which addresses these limitations through intrinsic and extrinsic reasoning within a shared chemical and conformational latent space. The latent space encompasses standard and modified amino acids, sugars, DNA, and RNA, with force-field supervision favoring physically plausible atomic reconstructions. Within this space, intrinsic reasoning uses recurrent refinement to adaptively allocate computation, while extrinsic reasoning guides search with arbitrary constraints such as energetic or geometric criteria. Across in silico protein design benchmarks, RFD4-Proteina achieves higher design success rates at greater generation throughput than all previous methods evaluated, with further gains from conformational flexibility, recurrent refinement, and search. The same model performs equivalently to or better than state-of-the-art specialist methods for side-chain packing, sequence design, conformational sampling, and design refinement. We demonstrate the power and versatility of RFD4-Proteina experimentally by designing specific and cross-reactive binders to therapeutically relevant targets, recognizing phosphorylations, controlling glycosylation, and creating enzymes that catalyze both bond-breaking and bond-forming reactions, including a first proof-of-concept demonstration of a de novo designed enzyme for active pharmaceutical ingredient synthesis. By unifying diverse chemistry, conformational flexibility, and scalable reasoning in a single physically grounded latent space, RFD4-Proteina expands the frontier of biomolecular design.

papers.title: Pallatom2: Navigating the De Novo Protein Universe with Atom-to-Atom Modeling
papers.abstract: Protein binder design requires precise coordination of molecular structure, binding geometry, and experimentally measurable performance. We introduce Pallatom2, an efficient, precise Atom-to-Atom generative model that jointly models protein sequence, backbone conformation, side-chain geometry, and target-interface contacts. A unified Atom14 representation and residue-guided sparse all-atom attention enable bidirectional information exchange between residue-level and atom-level representations, coordinating global structure with local atomic detail in a compact model of just 65.9 million parameters. Its conditioning system provides fine-grained control over binder-target engagement and global and local protein conformations, supporting diverse target-specific design requirements. In silico evaluation demonstrates broad generative capability across long-chain monomers, multi-domain proteins, and homomultimers, with monomer sampling extending to 1,600 residues. In binder design, Pallatom2 achieves state-of-the-art in silico screening performance across all nine targets with cross-method benchmark data under the reported protocols. These in silico results translate into substantial experimental success: biolayer interferometry identifies 112 active designs among 210 tested candidates (53.3%), with binders obtained for all ten experimentally evaluated targets. Six targets yield picomolar-scale apparent affinities, including K_D values of 3.96 pM for SC2RBD and 33.8 pM for PD-L1, while TNF reaches 1.166 nM. Beyond de novo discovery, starting-interface-guided BCMA design preserves association kinetics despite substantial sequence divergence; partial diffusion improves TNF affinity by up to 7.57-fold; and CDR-associated interface remodeling converts an inactive de novo nanobody into binders with apparent K_D values of 4.31 and 5.93 nM. Together, these results establish Pallatom2 as a versatile model for protein design, combining efficient atomic modeling, leading in silico screening performance, and experimentally demonstrated capabilities in high-affinity binder discovery, interface transfer, affinity maturation, and recovery of inactive designs.

papers.title: Machine Learning-Enhanced Mucosal Luminal Interface Metaproteomics Reveals Diagnostic Potential of Microbial Proteins in Pediatric Inflammatory Bowel Disease
papers.abstract: Abstract: Background: Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD), a chronic gastrointestinal disorder with two main subtypes, Crohn's Disease (CD) and Ulcerative Colitis (UC), is associated with more aggressive phenotypes and greater diagnostic complexity in pediatric patients. Conventional diagnostic biomarkers, lack sufficient distinguishing power between IBD subtypes. This study aimed to investigate and compare proteomic and metaproteomic profiles of pediatric IBD (PIBD) patients and healthy controls to develop a diagnostic panel capable of accurately diagnose IBD and distinguish its subtypes. Methods: We performed an in-depth evaluation of mucosal luminal interface samples from PIBD patients and healthy individuals, separately analyzing both the human proteome and microbial metaproteome data. The study involved selecting appropriate protein sets, employing feature selection techniques and machine learning across three intestinal regions: the terminal ileum, ascending colon, and descending colon. Results: Notably, panels composed solely of microbial biomarkers outperformed both human-only and combined human-microbial panels, achieving highly accurate results. Furthermore, the ascending colon emerged as the optimal sampling site, a result that aligns with the rich microbial diversity revealed in its taxonomic profile. Conclusions: Using a machine learning-based strategy on combined proteomics and metaproteomics, this study uncovered disease-relevant signaling pathways and delivered taxonomic as well as functional insights into the microbial dysbiosis of PIBD. A diagnostic panel built around microbial proteins (particularly those originating from the ascending colon) emerges as a promising tool for more precise stratification of PIBD subtypes. Larger, prospective studies are now needed to validate these candidate biomarkers and translate them into clinically deployable diagnostic panels. Keywords: Metaproteome, Biomarker, Pediatric Inflammatory bowel disease, Machine learning, Mucosal luminal interface.

papers.title: Unlocking Programmable and Creative RNA Sequence Design with RDiffusion
papers.abstract: RNA, a pillar of the central dogma, has shaped three billion years of evolution. Despite cataloging tens of millions of non-coding RNAs and annotating millions, we have barely scratched the surface of the vast, unexplored RNA sequence space. Here, we introduce RDiffusion, a discrete-diffusion-based generative transformer model for RNA sequence design. Conditioned on diverse biological features, such as desired function, family type, secondary and tertiary structure, or binding protein partners, it can guide the generation of novel RNA sequences tailored to specific design specifications. We evaluate RDiffusion across a broad spectrum of RNA design tasks and find that it not only surpasses all baseline methods in design success rate and sequence diversity but also achieves advanced performance on downstream tasks. To demonstrate its translational potential, we applied RDiffusion with a customized seed-screening pipeline to de novo design therapeutic MicroRNA(miRNA) mimics in osteoarthritis (OA). This strategy identified mimic 0-4 as a lead candidate targeting SDC4 to preserve ECM homeostasis and cartilage integrity, with robust efficacy validated in clinical OA samples. Altogether, RDiffusion holds strong potential to serve as a cornerstone for RNA generation and representation learning, establishing a generalizable AI-driven paradigm for RNA therapeutic discovery.

papers.title: Label-Free Lymphocyte Subtype and State Classification by Stimulated Raman Scattering Microscopy
papers.abstract: Accurate immune cell subtype and functional state profiling are essential for studying immune regulation, disease progression, and therapeutic response. Established single-cell analysis techniques rely heavily on either endpoint, destructive measurements or complex labeling that can potentially affect cell functions. Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy offers quantitative, label-free imaging of cells and tissues by providing contrast based on subcellular concentrations of intrinsic biomolecules at high spatial and temporal resolution. Here, we demonstrate that Vision Transformer based hyperspectral SRS imaging classification can accurately and non-destructively classify various lymphocyte phenotypes, including lymphocyte lineage (T and B cells), T cell subset and differentiation state (CD4+ and CD8+ T cells, effector, memory, and naive for both), and functional states (naive T, activated T, exhausted T) using fluorescent markers for training. By leveraging attention-based spatial-spectral feature learning, the approach captures biomolecular patterns associated with immune cell identity and state while preserving cells for downstream or longitudinal analysis. This provides a potential platform for label-free immune profiling, live-cell analysis, and longitudinal studies of immune cell type and state transitions.

papers.title: Savant: A Fast, Structure-Free Binding Affinity Predictor For Protein-Ligand Drug Screening
papers.abstract: Protein-ligand binding affinity determines which of many candidate molecules is worth synthesizing and assaying, making it the central measurement in early drug discovery. Binding affinity is commonly expressed as the dissociation constant, an equilibrium measure that indicates how easily a complex separates into its components. AI-based generative chemistry and make-on-demand chemical catalogs now produce molecules faster than rigorous method can evaluate them. Leading computational methods co-fold the complex before scoring the binding affinity between the protein and the ligand, which provides high accuracy but requires a graphics processing unit (GPU) and substantial time for every pair evaluated.Here we present Savant, a machine learning model that estimates the dissociation constant using only the protein's amino acid sequence and the ligand's structure written as a line of text (SMILES). Savant needs no 3-dimensional folded structure, no docking, and no GPU. To test Savant fairly, we built a benchmark designed to prevent any training data to leak into the testing set, drawing only on measurements published after the training data was assembled and on molecules chemically unlike anything the model had seen. On an independent benchmark, Savant ranks ahead of every other 3-dimensional structure-free method.Savant is designed to rank compounds against a single protein, and performs as well as other methods that require a GPU, while running only on a central processing unit (CPU). Thus, Savant can screen libraries of 100,000 compounds in minutes with commodity hardware.

papers.title: Spatially-Organized Adaptive Immune Niches in Granulomas Dictate Local Defense and Correlate with Disease Severity in Tuberculosis Patients
papers.abstract: The cellular composition and spatial organization of immune responses within tuberculosis (TB) granulomas have been increasingly characterized, yet how these spatially organized immune cell populations coordinate local adaptive immunity remains largely unknown. Here, we integrated single-cell multi-omics, spatial transcriptomics, and immune receptor profiling to construct a comprehensive spatial atlas of human TB granulomas. We identified two concentric adaptive immune niches surrounding the central necrotic core. The outer niche comprised granuloma-associated tertiary lymphoid structures (TLSs) that supported TFH-B cell interactions and exhibited functional germinal center-like features associated with antigen-driven B-cell maturation toward FCRL5 antibody-producing cells. The inner niche contained antigen-experienced and Mtb-reactive effector memory CD8 T cells (TEM), which were recruited from distal lung regions by LGALS9high chemokine-expressing macrophages and activated to undergo local clonal expansion. In lgals9l1 deficient zebrafish, macrophage depletion was accompanied by marked reductions in T- and B-cell enrichment within granulomas and increased bacterial loads, supporting a role for LGALS9high macrophages in coordinating local adaptive immunity against TB infection. Finally, AI-based prediction of spatial gene expression from clinical hematoxylin and eosin-stained specimens revealed that inferred TLS abundance increased with TB disease severity. These findings identify spatially interconnected adaptive immune niches that organize protective immune responses within human TB granulomas, therefore providing a foundation for understanding granuloma adaptive immunity and developing host-directed therapies and vaccines for TB (https://tbomics.smart-nbc.org.cn/).

papers.title: p53 supports healthy aging
papers.abstract: p53 is a master regulator of cellular stress responses that is also implicated in the aging process. Its role in aging is often considered an example of antagonistic pleiotropy (AP), where it acts beneficially as a tumor suppressor early in life, but detrimentally in late life, for example by driving accumulation of stress-associated, pro-inflammatory senescent cells. However, the causal role of p53 in aging is not well-defined, and the AP model has not been definitively tested through loss- of-function studies. Here we show, contrary to the prediction of AP, that p53 promotes healthy aging in mouse liver by suppressing excessive inflammation and maintaining metabolic function. Multimodal RNA, protein, epigenetic and spatial profiling at the single-cell level in aged mouse liver confirmed age-dependent increase in p53 pathway activation. Hepatocyte-specific knockout of p53 in livers of aged mice, but not of young mice, increased inflammation and immune infiltration. Mechanistically, p53 suppressed DNA replication stress and DNA damage, known precursors to inflammatory signaling. In aged hepatocytes, p53 also directly targeted and maintained expression of metabolic genes, and knockout of p53 sensitized aged mice to metabolic stress-induced liver damage. Complementing these loss-of-function data, pharmacological activation of p53 with the small-molecule MDM2 inhibitor HDM201 in aged mice reversed age-associated suppression of metabolic genes, decreased age-associated inflammation and delayed onset of frailty. These results identify p53 activity in aged tissue as protective rather than degenerative. Importantly, this protective function is pharmacologically targetable, potentially for the benefit of healthy aging in humans.

papers.title: Generative Data Augmentation for Small-Cohort Glioblastoma Diagnosis from Circulating microRNA: Why Same-Modality Validation Overstates Performance
papers.abstract: Circulating microRNAs (miRNAs) have potential as minimally invasive biomarkers for glioblastoma (GBM), but the small size of discovery groups makes it difficult to develop a classifier. The discovery cohort, GSE122488, comprised 38 patients (n = 38). Generative data augmentation was applied to increase the dataset, although evaluations based on held-out samples from the same cohort or a single validation set make it difficult to distinguish biological signals from cohort- or platform-specific effects. CTGAN and Tabular Variational Autoencoder (TVAE) models were trained on the 38-patient cohort producing 500 synthetic samples each. Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers were trained on augmented datasets and assessed using an escalating validation approach: first on an independent plasma cohort of the same modality (GSE184472, n = 118), and then on a tissue cohort from a different platform (Chinese Glioma Genome Atlas (CGGA), n = 198). XGBoost using TVAE-augmented data achieved an AUROC of 0.59 (95% CI 0.49-0.70) on GSE184472, compared with 0.42 to 0.53 without augmentation, although no AUROC on this cohort was significantly different from chance. However, this improvement did not carry to CGGA, where AUROC was 0.40 (95% CI 0.32-0.48) before harmonisation and 0.47 after Min-Max harmonisation. After harmonisation, a recall of 1.00 resulted from predicting every sample as GBM, leading to an accuracy of 0.41 and showing poor discrimination. The generalisation gap was examined in terms of modality mismatch, differing class definitions between cohorts, synthetic-data-related class imbalance, and incomplete cross-platform harmonisation. These findings show the need for independent, cross-platform validation before using data augmentation for diagnosis. The escalating validation framework provides a way to evaluate generalizability in small-cohort studies.

papers.title: Targeting Cellular Pseudo-Senescence to Overcome PARP inhibitors Resistance in BRCA1-Mutated Breast Cancer
papers.abstract: Poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors (PARPi) are a mainstay therapy for homologous recombination (HR)-deficient cancers; however, resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Previously, through a genome wide CRISPR screen, we identified ZNF251 haploinsufficiency as a novel driver of PARPi resistance. In BRCA1-mutant (BRCA1mut) cells, ZNF251 deficiency led to HR hyperactivation, conferring PARPi resistance that could be reversed by RAD51 inhibition. In this study, we further show that ZNF251 deficiency induces replication stress and a pseudo-senescence state, in which cells exhibit molecular and phenotypic markers of senescence while retaining proliferative capacity. Because senomorphic and senolytic therapies can target senescent cells, we tested whether these approaches could overcome PARPi resistance in ZNF251-deficient breast cancer cells. Critically, targeting this senescence-like state with either senomorphic agents, such as cytokine inhibitors, or senolytic agents, such as BCL-2 and BCL-XL inhibitors, overcame PARPi resistance ex vivo and in vivo. Importantly, pseudo-senescence was also observed in other PARPi-resistant contexts driven by HR hyperactivation, including 53BP1- and Shieldin-mutant cells, suggesting that it may represent a broader mechanism underlying PARPi resistance in breast cancer. Furthermore, in two olaparib-resistant, BRCA-mutant triple-negative breast cancer organoid models, treatment with DT2216, a BCL-XL targeting PROTAC, sensitized both models to olaparib. Together, our work defines a novel pathway linking HR hyperactivation, replication stress, and pseudo-senescence, and positions both senomorphic and senolytic therapies as promising strategies to overcome PARPi resistance in BRCA1mut breast cancer.

papers.title: Saturation mutagenesis and NMR of a fold switch reveal position-dependent deep learning performance
papers.abstract: A predictive understanding of the properties of fold-switching or metamorphic proteins can provide insights into protein dynamics and energetics, and enable the design of complex protein functions and molecular machines. Recently developed deep learning modeling tools, including AlphaFold, have led to dramatic increases in structural modeling accuracy, but their performance for prediction of fold switching or point mutant effects is unclear. Here we used NMR to measure all substitutions at three key positions of the GA/GB fold switch that differentially adopt -helical (3), {beta}-grasp (4{beta}+), or unfolded states, generating a quantitative experimental benchmark for mutation-level fold switching. Using this dataset to assess and compare a panel of deep learning and physics-based modeling and design algorithms, we identified variable and position-dependent performance across methods. Some AlphaFold2-based algorithms were able to predict mutant effects at individual sites, indicating partial sensitivity to physical effects of residue substitutions. Additional comparisons of predictions with experimentally measured stability changes further highlighted position-dependent success and general challenges for predictive algorithms. Together, this study provides a rigorous new benchmark for mutation-induced fold switching and reveals the capabilities and limitations of current deep learning models, establishing a foundational baseline for facilitating the next generation of prediction tools.

papers.title: Elflow: Automated Quality Control and Self-Supervised Representation Learning for High-Dimensional Cytometry
papers.abstract: High-dimensional flow and mass cytometry are foundational technologies for clinical immunophenotyping and hematological diagnostics, yet computational data analysis remains bottlenecked by operator-subjective manual gating. While computational tools have emerged, they remain fragmented across isolated tasks such as quality control or discrete clustering, leaving an unmet need for integrated, modular workflows that resolve continuous biological variation without manual supervision. Here, we introduce Elflow, a modular, self-supervised framework that links automated quality control, single-cell representation learning, and patient-level modeling without manual gating at inference. Elflow couples automated machine-learning quality control with Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization (VICReg) to learn continuous, batch-resilient single-cell representations without negative pairs or hand-labeled training sets. Across four diverse public benchmarks, Elflow adapts to distinct biological panels and clinical objectives. On 22-channel spectral flow cytometry (OMIP-030), self-supervised embeddings preserve fine functional T-cell gradations and outperform classical baselines in unsupervised clustering, while an anchor-guided extension accurately reproduces canonical manual gating hierarchies. On hand-curated CyTOF panels (Levine-13), linear PCA matches deep models, establishing an empirical boundary condition where linear methods suffice. Across multi-center clinical cohorts (FlowCAP-II), Elflow representations achieve high diagnostic sensitivity for acute myeloid leukemia across heterogeneous instruments despite severe class imbalance. In longitudinal immune monitoring (FlowCAP-IV), patient mean embeddings and micro-cluster differential histograms preserve rare antigen-specific responses, yielding significant AIDS-free survival stratification. By uniting automated quality control, self-supervised representation learning, and multi-scale patient aggregation, Elflow provides a modular, reproducibly benchmarked framework for high-parameter and multi-center translational cytometry.

papers.title: MtbAIM: AI/ML-guided endpoint-specific prediction of small-molecule activity across drug-susceptible and drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis
papers.abstract: The emergence of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) presents a major challenge to drug discovery, as compounds active against drug-susceptible (DS) isolates may not retain comparable inhibitory activity against drug-resistant (DR) isolates. Here, we developed an AI/ML workflow to independently prioritize small molecules separately against DS and DR isolates of M.tb and predict MIC, MIC90, and MIC99 as distinct quantitative endpoints. Following curation of data retrieved from the ChEMBL repository, molecular-activity datasets comprised 25,645 and 3,749 compounds tested against whole cell DS and DR isolates respectively. Molecular representations were generated using RDKit descriptors and Morgan fingerprints, along with embeddings from ChemBERTa, MolCLR, and Uni-Mol, and evaluated for binary activity classification and endpoint-specific regression. The best-performing DS classifier combined RDKit/Morgan features with ExtraTrees (balanced accuracy 0.782; AUROC 0.864; AUPRC 0.870), while histogram gradient boosting using the same features performed best for DR classification (balanced accuracy 0.762; AUROC 0.836; AUPRC 0.880). Similarly, RDKit/Morgan features combined with tree-based regressors achieved the best overall performance across all six DS/DR regression endpoints, with pooled out-of-fold RMSE values ranging from 0.604 to 0.784 pMIC units. To facilitate broader application, we developed MtbAIM (https://github.com/jasdeep002/MtbAIM), a Google Colab-based prediction platform that enables users to assess and prioritize small molecules against DS and DR isolates of M.tb.

papers.title: Thermodynamic, Kinetic, and Structural Basis of Polyspecificity in the Malaria Sugar Transporter PfHT1
papers.abstract: The malaria parasite Plasmodium falciparum relies on the polyspecific sugar transporter PfHT1 for survival in diverse nutrient environments, making the molecular basis of its polyspecificity a potential avenue for antimalarial drug discovery. However, the structural, thermodynamic and kinetic basis of the emergence of polyspecificity in membrane transporters are not established in literature. Despite advances in AI for protein engineering, the design of selective/promiscuous membrane transporter proteins remains challenging as it requires connecting substrate recognition to the energetics of the transport cycle. Here, we examine the molecular origins of polyspecificity in PfHT1 transporter using molecular dynamics simulations of substrate transport and experimental validation of the key residues that tune specificity. From a structural viewpoint, we hypothesize that polyspecific membrane transporter contains flexible structural elements that could reshape the binding pocket in a substrate-dependent manner. For PfHT1, the cracking of the extracellular helix TM7b allows flexible reshaping of the binding pocket similar to the promiscuous enzymes. The thermodynamic signature of polyspecificity emerges in the form of the substrate dependent stabilization of transport-competent states. From a kinetic perspective, this stabilization asymmetrically alters transition kinetics and channels the flux through diverse conformational pathways that facilitate the conformational transitions from outward to inward facing states. To investigate the contribution of the underlying interaction network to sugar specificity, we used graph-attention learning to prioritize mutant transporters with distinct substrate preferences. Distinct glucose- and fructose-dependent growth phenotypes identify positions with differential effects on sugar utilization, providing functional evidence relevant to substrate specificity within the polyspecific transporter. Together, these findings support a mechanism in which structural, thermodynamic and kinetics observables connect polyspecificity to conformational energetics, kinetics, and structural plasticity.

papers.title: LabARIA: A Multi-Agent System for Integrative Analytics in Clinical Laboratories
papers.abstract: BackgroundLaboratory medicine underpins clinical decision-making across nearly every care setting. Clinical laboratory errors and delays can compromise diagnostic reliability and patient care. However, laboratory quality and operational data are commonly reviewed through separate manual workflows, limiting timely recognition of emerging problems across complementary data sources. MethodsWe developed and evaluated LabARIA (Laboratory Agentic Reasoning and Integrative Analytics), a multi-agent AI system for coordinated surveillance of specimen workflows, analytical quality control, and laboratory operations. We conducted a single-center retrospective system development and evaluation at NewYork-Presbyterian Hospital/Weill Cornell Medical Center using laboratory data collected from May 1 through June 18, 2026, including 177,480 specimen-panel records, 75,103 internal quality-control (IQC) measurements, 633 proficiency-testing challenges, and 422 recalibration or maintenance actions. Forecasting agents were evaluated using patient-result streams with controlled perturbations, and synthetic staffing and inventory data. We assessed specimen rejection, cancellation, and turnaround-time patterns; warning recall and lead time before documented laboratory actions; assay-specific patient-based real-time quality control (PBRTQC) performance; and exploratory operational forecasting discrimination. FindingsLabARIA characterized specimen and workflow patterns across clinical units and time periods, including hemolysis-related potassium rejections in the intensive care unit during early morning hours (49 of 367 tests [13.3%]). For analytical quality monitoring, the IQC agent generated warnings before 407 of 422 recorded QC actions (recall, 0.964 [95% CI, 0.942-0.978]), with a median lead time of 5.40 days (95% CI, 3.75-6.07). PBRTQC agent selected different monitoring strategies across 35 analytes. In a separate analysis, adding PBRTQC increased action recall from 0.964 to 0.993 (95% CI, 0.979-0.998). A dashboard presented tiered alerts for human review, and an accompanying chatbot supported interactive exploration of the summaries. For the operational forecasting module, areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve for 7-day inventory and staffing risk forecasting were 0.800 (95% CI, 0.696-0.881) and 0.877 (95% CI, 0.778-0.950), respectively. InterpretationLabARIA demonstrated the feasibility of coordinating laboratory quality surveillance across heterogeneous data sources, providing a foundation for intelligent clinical laboratories. Prospective studies are warranted to determine whether this approach improves monitoring beyond conventional methods, supports laboratory decisions, and benefits patient care without excessive alert burden.
